Lesson Proper

A. Introduction: The Benefits of Green Manure Crops in Improving Soil Fertility

Farm soil is an invaluable asset to farmers. Managing it sustainably is essential not
only for current crop production but also for ensuring productivity for future
generations. Once soil is degraded, restoring its capacity is extremely difficult and
often takes many years. Maintaining healthy soil, therefore, is the key to successful
vegetable production, especially under a protected facility such as greenhouse.

Green manure crops are plants grown specifically to be incorporated into the soil to
enhance fertility and improve soil structure. These crops are typically fast-growing
and may include legumes, grasses, or other species. Legumes are highly valued for
their ability to fix atmospheric nitrogen, thereby enriching the soil with this essential
nutrient.

Green manure crops are usually grown directly in the target field. However, if this is
not possible, biomass harvested from other areas can be incorporated into the soil.
With this latter method, though, some of the benefits provided by the crop’s roots –
such as nematode suppression and nitrogen fixation – may not be realized.

To start, we will first explore the properties of soil, its aggregate structure and
examine how green manuring can improve these properties.

1. Soil Properties

Soil is a complex resource. It has chemical, physical and biological properties, and
these influence one another. The combination and balance of these properties
determine the productivity of the soil.

 Chemical properties – include soil pH (acidity) and the amount of
nutrients present.
 Physical properties – include soil structure, hardness, aggregate
structure, water infiltration rate, aeration and drainage condition.
 Biological properties – include organic matter, soil microorganisms, and
plant roots

Figure 1. Soil Properties

### PDF Page 41

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=41

2. Soil Aggregate Structure

One of the most important properties of the soil is its aggregate structure. Soil
aggregate structed are assembled by particles of sand, silt and clay and can occur
in different patterns which results in different soil structures. Well-aggregated
soil has high capacity of holding nutrients and water. It can also improve aeration
and drainage. With a good aggregate structure, plant roots can grow deeper and
stronger.

Figure 2. Soil Aggregate Structure

Green manuring is one of the most effective and practical methods to maintain
the good balance of soil properties. The effects may vary depending on the type
of green manure crop used and the common benefits are as follows:
 Improve soil physical properties – makes the soil softer and easier for roots
to grow
 Increase soil organic matters – adds food organisms and improves soil
fertility
 Increase soil nitrogen contents – legumes supply this important nutrient
for the crop
 Control weeds – fast-growing green manure crops cover the soil and
suppress weed growth
 Prevent soil erosion – plant cover protects the soil from being washed away
by rain of blow by the wind

B. Types of Green Manure Crops

There are several types of crops which can be used for green manuring, each with its
own characteristics and effects. Therefore, when introducing green manuring, it is
important to carefully select the crop type based on the environmental conditions and
the specific purpose of its use. Below are some examples of green manure crops and
their characteristics.

### PDF Page 42

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=42

1. Leguminous green manure crops
Leguminous crops, such as clover and crotalaria, are commonly used as green
manure because of their ability to fix air nitrogen through rhizobium bacteria in
their roots, thereby improving soil fertility.

Their main benefits include:

- Nitrogen fixation – rhizobium bacteria on their roots capture nitrogen
from the air and convert it into a form that plants can use.
- Rapid nutrient release – legume residues decompose quickly, making
nutrients readily available for the crop.
- Weed control – their dense canopy growth can suppress weed
development.

In addition, some leguminous green manure crops help suppress nematode
populations, while others promote mycorrhiza development, which improves
phosphorus uptake by plants. The table below are examples of common
leguminous green manure crops and their benefits.

- Nitrogen Fixation

2. Gramineous (Grass family) green manure crops

Gramineous crops, such as sorghum and oats, are also widely utilized as green
manure.

Their main benefits include:

- Soil structure improvement - their dense, fibrous root systems enhance
soil aggregation.
- Increase in soil organic matter - their large above-ground biomass and
root residues contribute significant organic matter when incorporated.
- Nutrient cycling – they capture nutrients from deeper layers of soil and
gradually release them back as they decompose.

Table 2 are examples of common gramineous green manure crops and their
benefits.

3. Other Green Manure Crops

Aside from legumes and gramineous crops, there are also other plants used as
green manuring (Table 3). Examples include sunflower, mustard seeds, certain
types of radishes and buckwheat.

Their main benefits include:

- Nutrient cycling – deep taproots, such as those of radish, can absorb
nutrients from deeper soil layers, reduce nutrient leaching and make
them available for the next crop.

organic matter to the soil and improve soil fertility.

D. Application of Green Manure Crops

There is a common method of growing and incorporating green manure crops into
the soil. Application of Mokusaku (wood vinegar) and Carbonized Rice Hull (CRH)
together with green manure crops is also recommended. Mokusaku has been used as
a natural pesticide and fungicide, and as a soil conditioner. CRH is an effective soil
amendment due to its porous structure. It improves soil structure and provides
habitat for beneficial microorganisms.

Steps in Applying Green Manure Crops:
1. Irrigate the field adequately to moisten the soil.
2. Broadcast the seeds at the recommended rate.
3. Cover the seeds with 1-5 cm soil (depending on the seed size) or mix lightly
with a rake.
4. Press the soil to ensure good seed-to-soil contact.
5. Allow the crop to grow for 1.5-2 months, depending on the type of crop.
6. Incorporate the plants into the soil before or at the start of flowering, but
always before seed setting. If plants are too tall, chop them into smaller
pieces.
7. Spray Mokusaku (wood vinegar) when the green manure crop is mixed.
8. Mix the CRH with the green manure.
9. Wait for at least 2 weeks, ideally for 4 weeks, before planting the main
crop.

Figure 3 shows an example of the on-farm demonstration using Crotalaria for soil
conditioning in greenhouse. Any locally available green manure materials can be
used as an alternative of Crotalaria.
 Seeds were sown on February 5.
 Incorporation of Crotalaria and application of CRH were done on March
27.
 Recommended seeding rate is 100 kg/ha (10 g/m2).
 Recommended CRH rate is 1 kg/m2 (dry) or 5 L/m2.
 Crotalaria was incorporated twice using a hand tractor.
 After CRH application, the soil was tilled two more times.

Summary

Green manuring is a sustainable and biological method for maintaining healthy soil, which
is essential for successful vegetable production. In this lesson, we discussed the benefits
of green manuring crops and learned the practical steps in applying green manuring.

When using this method, there are few key points to consider:
- Selection of crop type – clearly know the purpose of green manuring and select
what is best suited to the local climate and soil conditions.
- Timing – analyze and properly plan the cropping pattern and calendar to include
green manuring. Allow at least 2 weeks, ideally 4 weeks, between mixing the
green manure crops into the soil and planting the main vegetables.

Soil Analysis and Fertilizer Recommendation

This lesson provides essential knowledge and skills for improving soil quality. It focuses
on the proper collection of soil samples, the use of a Soil Test Kit (STK) for nutrient
analysis, and the computation of recommended fertilizer application rates for tomato and

Lesson Objective

and nutrient status and compute appropriate fertilizer recommendations for
tomatoes and sweet pepper.

Specifically, the participants should be able to:
1. conduct soil sampling;
2. perform soil analysis with the use of Soil Test Kit (STK); and
3. compute the recommended fertilizer application rate of each crop.

Opener

Title: The Doctor’s Check-up
Time allotment:5 minutes
Materials needed: None

Procedure
1. Facilitator says:
“Before we begin, let me ask you something. What’s the first thing a
doctor usually does before giving a patient medicine?”
2. Allow participants to answer.
(Possible Answers: ‘Check your temperature,’ ‘Ask questions,’ ‘Do tests,’
‘Find out what’s wrong,’ etc.)
3. Facilitator continues: “That’s right. A doctor doesn’t just give medicine
right away. They examine the patient and may even request laboratory
tests to know exactly what the problem is. Only then do they
recommend the right treatment or dosage.”
4. Ask: “Now imagine if a doctor prescribed medicine without checking
your condition first — what could happen?”
(Encourage a few short answers, e.g., ‘It might make things worse,’ ‘The
medicine could be wrong,’ etc.)

Key Message to be derived:
“Soil testing allows us to make informed decisions. Just as a medical check-up ensures
the right treatment for our bodies, soil analysis ensures the right nutrients for our
crops — leading to healthier soil, better yields, and more efficient fertilizer use.”

Connecting statement to the Lesson: “The same principle applies to our farms. We
can’t tell what the soil really needs just by looking at it. If we apply fertilizer without
testing, we might give too much or too little — just like giving the wrong medicine.
Soil analysis works like a ‘check-up’ for the soil, helping us understand its condition
before we ‘treat’ it with fertilizers.”

Lesson Proper

A. Introduction: Understanding the Soil and Soil Analysis

Soil is a dynamic natural body composed of mineral and organic materials and living
forms. It provides a medium for plant roots to anchor and supplies them with
essential nutrients, water, and air. It varies in texture (such as sand, silt, or clay),
structure, and fertility depending on its origin and environmental conditions. In
agriculture, soil health and quality are vital for sustainable crop production.

Soil fertility is the capacity of soil to provide the essential nutrients required by plants
for their growth and development. This includes macronutrients like nitrogen,
phosphorus, and potassium, as well as micronutrients such as iron, manganese,
copper and zinc.

One of the causes of low yields in the Philippines is low soil fertility. Continuous
cropping without replenishment of the soil nutrients inevitably results in the
depletion of its fertility. This is especially true of the high-yielding crop varieties now
grown. Every time a crop is harvested, the nutrients absorbed are removed from the
soil. With high yields, a corresponding high amount of nutrients is taken from the soil.
This natural depletion of nutrients by crops is aggravated in cases where proper soil
fertility management practices-fertilization and liming, proper tillage, crop rotation,
erosion control and organic matter maintenance are overlooked.

Farmers must understand the characteristics of the soil because it plays a vital role in
successful crop production. Different types of soil support different crops, and
knowing the soil’s texture, pH level, and nutrient content helps farmers choose the
most suitable vegetables to plant. Soil knowledge also allows farmers to maximize
crop yield and quality by applying the right type and amount of fertilizer. Proper soil
management helps prevent degradation and ensures long-term productivity.
Understanding the soil leads to better resource use, helping farmers save money on
fertilizers and inputs while protecting the environment. Soil is also an irreplaceable
asset for farmers.

One way to understand the soil is through soil analysis. Soil analysis helps farmers
diagnose their soil problems before planting, allowing for smart decisions on fertilizer
use, crop selection, and soil improvement. By tracking the exact amount of soil
nutrients, it can easily adjust fertilization in accordance with soil and crop
requirements. Using farm management, farmers can take advantage of getting
fertilizer recommendations based on data that increases plant growth for optimum
yield. Additionally, soil analysis facilitates crop nutrient management by revealing the
current soil pH level.

B. Soil Sample Collection

One of the most important issues associated with soil testing is obtaining a
good soil sample that represents the area to be tested.

The main objective of soil sampling is to collect a small amount of soil sample
weighing about ½ to 1kg that will represent the soil in a large area. Since only
a small amount of soil sample is used in chemical analysis and results are

C. Conduct of Soil Analysis through Soil Test Kit (STK)

Soil laboratory chemical analysis takes a long time to finish and requires costly
chemicals, technical manpower, and instruments. Soil Test Kit (STK) is a less costly
and rapid procedure that results in the qualitative interpretation of the relative
amounts of plant nutrients. Analysis by the Soil Test Kit is a quick method of
evaluating fertility status of the soil. In the Philippines, the standard Soil Test Kit (STK)
developed by UPLB and produced and distributed by the Bureau of Soils and Water
Management (BSWM) is commonly used.

Figure 10. Soil Test Kit (left). Comparing the Color of Soil Sample to the Chart (right)

Important Reminders when using STK

Soil pH

Soil pH is a measure of the degree of acidity or alkalinity. A pH of 7 is neutral. The
lower the pH (below 7), the more acidic the soil is. On the other hand, the higher the
pH (above 7) the soil becomes more alkaline.

Soil pH is important due to its influence on the uptake of soil nutrients. The main
purpose of managing soil pH is to be able to adjust the acidity to the point where there
are no toxic metals exposed to the crops, as well as to ensure that nutrient availability
is at its maximum.

Soil pH can be analyzed with the use of the Soil Test Kit or with the use of a pH Paper
(Figure 11).

Figure 11. Analyzing soil pH using a pH Paper during a technical training in Japan.

Testing Soil pH using the Standard Soil Test Kit using the Updated Manual of STK
Distributed by BSWM
1. In a clean and dry test tube, transfer soil sample up to the first scratch mark
2. Fill the test tube with CPR reagent up to the second scratch mark.
3. Mix well by gently tapping the test tube into your palm for 1 minute. Make
sure to disturb the soil sample.
4. Stand the test tube for 2 minutes. Repeat step 3.
5. Stand the test tube for 5 minutes
6. Using a clean and white background, incline the test tube and match the
color of the resulting solution with the colors for CP in Figure 12.

Determination of Soil Nitrogen using STK
Procedure (Paningbatan et al., 1978)
1. In a clean and dry test tube, transfer soil sample up to the first scratch.
2. Fill the test tube with N reagent up to the second scratch mark.
3. Mix well by gently tapping the test tube into your palm for 1 minute. Make
sure to disturb the soil sample.
4. Stand the test tube for 5 minutes. Repeat step 3.
5. Heat the bottom of the test tube for about 30 seconds or until the solution
starts bubbling.
6. Stand the test tube for 2 minutes or until it has cooled down to room
temperature.
7. Using a clean and white background, incline the test tube and match the
color of the resulting solution with the colors in Figure 13.
8. Record the result of the analysis. Refer to the Soil Analysis and Fertilizer
Usage booklet for the computation of the fertilizer recommendation for
various crops.
9. Discard the solution in the appropriate waste container. Wash the test tube
and rinse using distiller water. Dry and store back in the STK bag.

Determination of Potassium using STK
1. In a clean and dry test tube (KT1), transfer soil sample up to the first scratch
mark.
2. Fill the test tube with K reagent up to the second scratch mark.
3. Mix well by gently tapping the test tube into your palm for about 1 minute.
4. Stand the test tube for 1 minute. Repeat step 3.
5. Stand the test tube for 5 minutes.
6. In a separate test tube (KT2), fill with K1 reagent up to the first scratch mark
and K2 up to the second scratch mark.
7. Mix well by gently tapping the test tube into your palm for 30 seconds.
8. Transfer aliquot from the first test tube (KT1) up to the third scratch mark
of the second test tube (KT2).
9. Mix well by gently tapping the test tube into your palm for 1 minute.
10. Using the provided purple background, observe the formation of a turbid
orange solution. Match the turbidity of the solution in Figure 15.
11. Record the result of the analysis. Refer to the Soil Analysis and Fertilizer
Usage booklet for the computation of the Fertilizer recommendation for

12. Discard the solution in the appropriate waster container. Wash the test tube
and rinse using distilled water. Dry and store back in the STK bag.

TEST Precautions when using the STK
a. Wear appropriate personal protective equipment before performing the
analysis.
b. Avoid inhalation and direct contact of chemicals with skin and eyes. Always
put the cap back on to prevent spillage and contamination of reagents.
c. Perform the analysis in a well-ventilated area with natural or white light
source to better visualize and compare the solutions to the color charts and
illustrations.
d. Store the reagents in a cool, dry place, and away from direct sunlight to
prevent degradation.
e. Always work under the fume hood when handling fuming chemicals and
concentrated acids.
f. Perform heating with care and caution.

D. Fertilizer Recommendation

It is important to emphasize that the result of soil testing is not the sole basis of
fertilizer recommendation. Other factors such as the cost of fertilizer in relation to
anticipated price of the product, expected yield, plant response to higher rates of
fertilizer, climatic conditions and other risks factors in crop production should be
considered by the farmer in determining the right kind of fertilizer to use.

Fertilizer is any substance solid or liquid, natural or synthetic, organic or inorganic,
single or combination of materials, applied directly to the soil or to the plants that
provides one or more of the essential nutrient elements to promote plant nutrition
and growth; thereby increasing crop yield and/or improve crop quality.

Fertilizer grade is the percentage of total Nitrogen (N), available phosphoric acid
(P2O5) and water-soluble potash (K2O) contained in the material. For example, a 14-
14-14 fertilizer has 14% N, 14% P2O5 and 14% K2O.

There are several kinds of compound chemical fertilizers such as;
14-14-14
16-16-16
30-45-40
90-60-30
46-0-0 (urea)
21-0-0 (ammonium sulfate)/21-0-0-0-24s
0-0-60 (potassium chloride)/ muriate of potash
0-22-0/0-20-0/0-18-0 or super phosphate
16-20-0 or ammonium phosphate

How to calculate the required amount of fertilizers based on the STK results

Below isa table showing the fertilizer recommendation for tomato and sweet pepper
lifted from the BSWM STK manual. Using this as reference, the following are examples
on how to calculate the recommended fertilizer rates based on STK results.

Table 5. Fertilizer recommendations based on quick Soil Test Kit

Example 1:
Crop: Tomato
STK Result: Soil has a pH of 5.8 or moderately acidic, low in nitrogen (N), high in
phosphorus (P₂O₅) and high in potassium (K₂O).

Referring to Table 5, the fertilizer recommendation for low nitrogen is 90 kg N/ha, for
high phosphorus is 30 kg P2O5/ha while for high potassium is 30 kg for K2O/ha. The
fertilizer recommendation for tomato will mainly focus on supplying nitrogen. Since
phosphorus and potassium are already abundant in the soil. If you use urea (which
contains 46% nitrogen) how much amount would be needed with 1 bagof urea (46-
0-0) weighing 50 kgs.

### PDF Page 66

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=66

Calculations:
1. To calculate the required weight of fertilizer, divide the amount of nutrient
needed by the nutrient content (percentage of the fertilizer material).

Wt. of fertilizer = amount of nutrient required x 100
Nutrient content

Wt. of urea (kg) = 90 = 90__ x 100
(46/100) 0.46
= 195. 65 kgs of urea/ha
(round off to nearest decimal place = 196)

2. To get the number of fertilizer bags, divide the total weight of nutrients
required by the weight of nutrient contained in one bag.

Number of fertilizer bags = weight of nutrient____
Weight of nutrient per bag

No. of bags = ___196 kgs____
50 kgs/bag
= 3.92 or 4 bags

Interpretation: To meet the 90 kg N/ha requirement, the farmer should apply
about 195 kgs or 4 bags of urea.

Example 2

The fertilizer recommendation calls for the application of 90 kg of N, 30 kg P2O5 and
30 kg of K2O of per hectare. Use the 14-14-14 and 21-0-0 as fertilizer sources.

Note that N, P2O5, K20 will be supplied by 14-14-14.
Wt. of 14-14-14 = 30 kg P/K/N x 100
= 214.3 kgs of 14-14-14

Since 14-14-14 contains N, P2O5 and K2O in the same amount and ratio, 214.3 kg will
supply 30 kg N, 30 kg P2O5, 30 kg K2O, the remaining amount of 60 kg N can then be
supplied by 21-0-0 fertilizer (ammonium sulfate).
Wt. of 21-0-0 = ___60____ x 100
= 285.7 kg of 21-0-0
The fertilizer recommendation of 90 kg of N, 30 kg of K2O and 30 kg of P2O5 per
hectare will then require 214.3 kg of 14-14-14 and 285.7 kg of 21-0-0 (ammonium
sulfate).

Summary

Soil sampling and analysis helps improve soil quality and ensure efficient crop production.
The use of Soil Test Kit (STK) helps determine soil nutrient levels and computation for the
appropriate fertilizer recommendation for crops. Regular soil testing is encouraged to
monitor changes in soil fertility and to guide future nutrient management decisions.

The proper use of fertilizer requires the ability to compute for the fertilizer need of a given
crop in a unit area. The amount of nutrient supplied must be in adequate amount and
suitable proportion. All soils which are originally fertile may lose these characteristics
because of improper soil and nutrient management.

Lesson 3

Grafting of Tomato Seedlings

Tomato grafting is a transformative agricultural practice for tomato cultivation. Grafting
involves joining a desirable tomato variety (scion) onto a robust root system (rootstock)
from another tomato variety or another crop, such as eggplant. This process combines the
best traits of both, leading to increased disease resistance, higher yields, and improved
plant vigor. With this lesson, learners will acquire the knowledge and practical skills
necessary to perform tomato grafting effectively, thereby contributing to increased
productivity and improved crop health.

Lesson Objective
At the end of the lesson, the participants should be able to demonstrate proper
skill in grafting tomato.

Specifically, the participants should be able to:
1. explain the benefits of tomato grafting and its importance in modern agriculture.
2. identify the key tools and materials needed for successful grafting.
3. perform the most common grafting methods with confidence.
4. describe the proper management techniques for grafted seedlings to ensure a
strong union.
5. recognize and avoid common pitfalls during the grafting and planting process.

Time Allotment: 5 hours
Methodologies: Lecture-discussion, open forum, demonstration and return
demonstration
Tools to Use: Laptop, LCD projector, PowerPoint (PPT) presentation and
demonstration materials

CONTENTS
A. Introduction to Tomato Grafting
B. Grafting Methods
C. Management After Grafting
D. Keys to Successful Grafting
E. Cautions When Planting Grafted Tomatoes

Title: Find the missing pieces
Time allotment: 5-7 minutes
Materials needed:
- Printed pictures of grafted tomato plants, each showing the joined scion and
rootstock.

- Envelopes or small containers to hold each set of puzzle pieces.
- Flat surface (tables or desks) for participants to assemble their puzzles.

Procedure
1. Introduce the activity by saying: “In tomato grafting, each part plays an
important role—the scion and the rootstock must fit perfectly for the plant
to grow strong. In this activity, we’ll see how important it is to find the right
connection by completing a puzzle of grafted tomato plants.”
2. Activity Proper (4-5 minutes)
- Divide participants into small groups.
- Give each group an envelope containing puzzle pieces of a grafted
tomato plant image-with one or two pieces missing.
- Distribute the missing pieces randomly among other groups.
- Instruct each group to find and trade the missing pieces that complete
their puzzle.

find the correct matching pieces.

- Once all puzzles are complete, have groups display their finished
images.

o "What did you notice about how each piece fit together?"
o "Why is it important for the scion and rootstock to connect
properly in grafting?"

Processing: Just like the puzzle, grafting requires the scion and rootstock to fit
perfectly at the graft union for nutrients and water to flow effectively. A poor
connection means the plant cannot grow well—just like a puzzle with missing or
mismatched pieces.

Connecting statement to the Lesson: This activity illustrates that every part of a
grafted plant has a specific role, and successful grafting depends on a precise and
compatible union between the scion and rootstock. As we move forward, we will
explore the actual steps and techniques used in tomato grafting to ensure a strong and
healthy union.

Lesson Proper

A. Introduction to Tomato Grafting

Tomato grafting is the process of joining the top part of one tomato variety (scion)
onto the root system of another variety (rootstock). The purpose is to combine the
desired fruit qualities of the scion with the rootstock’s superior resistance of soil-
borne diseases, as well as its vigor and stress tolerance. This results in a healthier,
and more productive plant. This process is particularly important when aiming for
long-term tomato production. This technique is widely used to prevent damage from
soil-borne diseases, especially in greenhouse cultivation where the same soil is used
repeatedly.

Before proceeding with grafting, it is essential to conduct pre-grafting activities,
which include the proper production of rootstock and scion seedlings. The activities
are as follows:

1. Seed Sowing and Timing

Staggered Sowing: Since the scion and rootstock varieties often have different
germination and growth rates, they should be sown on different dates. Generally,
the more vigorous rootstock seeds are sown a few days after the scion seeds to
ensure that both reach the same stem diameter at grafting time. However,
depending on the specific varieties used, sowing seeds of scion and rootstock on
the same day may also be appropriate. Because stem size is critical to successful
grafting, careful planning of the sowing schedule is essential. In general, 3-4
week-old seedlings are ideal for tube grafting.

Sufficient Seeds: Always sow more seeds than the exact number of grafted
plants required. This ensures a wider selection of healthy seedlings and increases
the likelihood of finding pairs with perfectly matched stem diameters for
grafting.

2. Growing Conditions

Optimal Environment: Provide ideal germination and growth conditions,
including a consistently warm temperature (around 85°F or 29°C for tomatoes)
and adequate light. A heat mat can be very helpful for germination.

Sterile Media: Use a fresh, sterile soilless medium to prevent soil-borne
diseases.

Cleanliness: Maintain a clean workspace and sanitize all tools and trays to avoid
the spread of pathogens.

Avoid Stress: Do not graft plants that are showing signs of disease, are stressed
from lack of water, or have become root-bound. Healthy seedlings are the
foundation of a healthy grafted plant.

### PDF Page 75

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=75

3. Watering and Fertilization

Uniform Watering: Ensure that both the scion and rootstock seedlings receive
consistent watering. However, experienced growers often reduce or withhold
irrigation for 1-2 days before grafting.

Why Reduce Water? This practice lowers the root pressure in the rootstock. If the
rootstock has too much water, a droplet can form on the cut surface, which can
interfere with the graft union and prevent it from healing properly.

Light Watering: On the day of grafting, ensure the potting mix is moist but not
saturated.

4. Matching Stem Diameters

The Golden Rule: The most critical factor for a successful graft is matching the
stem diameters of the scion and rootstock. They should be as close as possible to
ensure alignment of the vascular tissues.

How to Check: The best way to check is by using a grafting clip. If a clip of a certain
size (e.g., 1.5mm or 2.0mm) fits snugly on both stems, they are ready to graft.

Stem Firmness: Look for stems that are firm and sturdy, often with a slight
purplish color. Overly green, fast-growing stems may be too soft and fragile for a
strong graft.

B. Grafting Methods

For the grafting method, we will focus on two (2) of the most popular and effective
methods – tube and Approach grafting.

1. Tube Grafting (Splice Grafting). This is a simple and widely used grafting
method where both the scion and rootstock are cut at an angle, and a silicone
grafting clip or tube is used to hold them together. This method is fast but needs
intensive care after grafting for a high success rate. One of the advantages of this
methods is that it allows faster work efficiency, with 40-50 seedlings grafted per
hour per person. However, caring for the grafted seedlings is more challenging,
and they tend to have a lower survival rate.

Steps in Tube Grafting

Step 1: Cut the Rootstock and scion Stem. The first step is to cut both the
rootstock and the scion stems at a sharp, diagonal angle (Figure 1B). This deep
angled cut creates a larger surface area than a flat cut, allowing more contact
between the tissues of the rootstock and scion. This increased contact surface
promotes better fusion of cells, which is essential for successful graft healing.

Step 2. Place a Grafting Clip on the Rootstock. Second, after cutting the
rootstock, place a grafting clip halfway over the cut stem (Figure1C). It is
important to orient the grafting clip along the side of the graft cut so that it holds
the graft union securely.

come into contact sufficiently and may not heal (Figure 16B and 16C).

Tube Grafting of Tomato Seedling as shown in Figure 16 are the steps to follow
to get a desired fruit-bearing scion with a soil borne-disease resistant rootstock.
Prepare young seedlings and use a clean blade to make a slanted cut on both
plants. A small, flexible tube is then used to connect the cut ends, holding them
together. This ensures the inner layers of the stems touch so they can fuse. Finally,
support the new plant with a stick and place it in a humid environment to help it
heal and become a single, healthy plant.

Figure 17 shows the different cutting of rootstock. Cutting rootstock and scion
stems at different angles could result in graft failure. Figure 17A is an example of
a rootstock and scion cut at similar angles, an essential step to ensure graft
success. The cuts in Figure 17B and 17C does not match. These grafts are likely
to fail.

A B C

Figure 17. Cutting rootstock and scion stems.

2. Approach Grafting. This is a technique where two separate, still-rooted plants
are joined together until their stems fuse. Both plants remain on their own roots
during the healing process, which increases the chance of a successful union.
Once the stems are fused, the bottom of the scion and the top of the rootstock are
cut, resulting in a single plant with the desired characteristics from both.

Steps in Approach Grafting
Step 1: Choose and Prepare Plants
- Select two healthy tomato plants with different variety.
- Ensure that both plants are similar in size and planted close enough for
their stems to be easily joined.
- Remove the lower leaves that may obstruct or interfere the grafting site.

Step 2: Make Incisions
- On both plants, cut the stems at similar and approximately the same
height to prepare them for joining.
- On the rootstock, make a lengthwise cut from the top downward.
- On the scion, make a lengthwise cut from bottom upward.
- These opposite directions ensure a snug and secure mechanical fit
when the cut surfaces are joined.
- Each cut should extend slightly into the pith (center) of the stem, just
beyond the cambium layer, to promote effective tissue fusion.

### PDF Page 78

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=78

Step 3: Join and Secure
- Join the plants by bringing the cut surfaces of the scion and rootstock
into direct contact, ensuring precise alignment of the cuts.
- Secure the graft union firmly using grafting clips, grafting tape, or a
suitable wrapping material such as parafilm.
- Ensure proper contact between the vascular cambium layers of both
plants to facilitate the flow of water and nutrients and promote
successful graft union formation.

Step 4: Post-Graft Care
- Keep the grafted plants away from direct sunlight for approximately 15
days to minimize stress and promote healing.
- Maintain adequate moisture in the growing medium, ensuring it
remains moist but not waterlogged.
- Monitor the graft union for signs of successful fusion and growth. The
graft will take about 3-5 weeks to fully heal.

Step 5: Separate and Prune
- Once the graft union has fully healed and the two plants are growing as
one, cut the root of the scion plant to make it entirely dependent on the
rootstock for water and nutrient uptake.
- Remove any shoots that emerge below the graft union on the rootstock
below the graft union.

Grafting Tools and Materials

Here are the necessary tools and materials to be used for grafting.

- Scion and Rootstock Seedlings. Carefully selected seedlings of the same
stem diameter, typically with 2-4 true leaves.
- Sharp, Sterilized Blade. A new razor blade or a sharp grafting knife is
essential for making clean, precise cuts. Sterilization with rubbing alcohol is
critical to prevent the spread of diseases.
- Grafting Clips or Tubes. Small silicone or plastic clips that will hold the scion
and rootstock together firmly during the healing process.
- Barbecue sticks as support for the seedling.
- Seedling Trays. To hold the scion and rootstock seedlings before and after
grafting.
- Healing Chamber. A controlled environment with high humidity (90-
100%) and moderate temperatures (68-77°F or 20-25°C). This can be an
improvised plastic tent or a specialized grafting chamber.

Other Materials as shown in the Figure Below.

C. Management After Grafting

The period immediately following grafting is crucial for a successful union. Here are some
ways to manage after grafting.
- Healing Chamber: Immediately place the newly grafted plants in a high-
humidity healing chamber. The high humidity prevents the scion from wilting
while the vascular tissues of the scion and rootstock fuse.
- Light: Keep the plants in low light for the first 2-3 days, gradually increasing light
exposure over the next 7-10 days.
- Hardening Off: After the graft union has healed (typically 7-14 days), gradually
acclimate the plants to normal growing conditions by reducing humidity and
increasing light.
- Monitoring: Regularly check for signs of wilting, disease, or failed grafts.

Misting/ spraying: During the first 5-7 days after grafting, the scion has not yet
established a functional connection with the rootstock's water supply. Without an external
source of moisture, the scion would quickly dehydrate and die. Misting provides two
critical functions:

1. Reduces Transpiration: A high-humidity environment drastically reduces the
rate at which the scion's leaves lose water vapor.
2. Provides Water Source: Misting can provide a small amount of water that the
scion's leaves can absorb directly from the air, helping it stay hydrated until the
graft union is complete.

Misting and Spraying Tips
- Frequency: Misting should be most frequent during the first 2-3 days after
grafting, as this is the most critical and vulnerable period for the seedlings.
During this phase, misting may be done every few hours to maintain adequate
humidity. The frequency should then be gradually reduced as the graft union
begins to heal and the scion establishes a connection with the rootstock.
- Technique: Use a fine-mist sprayer. The goal is to create a fine fog or mist
around the plants, not to drench them. The spray should be directed over the
seedlings, allowing the mist to gently settle on the leaves.
- Target Area: Direct the mist toward the foliage and the air surrounding the
seedlings to maintain high humidity levels. Avoid spraying the graft union
directly, as excess moisture at the graft site can promote pathogen growth and
cause rotting.
- Controlled Environment: In modern commercial operations, a dedicated
healing chamber with automated misting system is used to precisely control
humidity (typically 90-100%) and temperature (20-28°C or 68-77°F). This
eliminates the need for manual spraying.

Figure 20 shows the step-by-step guide for creating a protected, low-stress environment
immediately after grafting, followed by a controlled transition to normal growing
conditions. This is divided into three key areas of care over an 11-day period.

### PDF Page 81

Figure 20. Schedule for post-grafting care
Source: S. Koyama, JICA Tsukuba (modified)

1. Water
- Days 0-6: "Hand spray" indicates that the seedlings should be lightly
misted with water. This is crucial for maintaining high humidity around
the graft, which prevents the scion from wilting before it can connect to
the rootstocks.
- Days 7-11: "Irrigate as required" shows a shift to normal watering. At this
point, the graft has begun to heal, and the plant can draw water from the
roots.

2. Plastic Cover
- Days 0-6: "Close completely" means the seedlings should be kept in a
sealed, high-humidity environment, such as a humidity chamber or under
a clear plastic cover. This seals in moisture and is essential for the initial
healing phase.
- Days 7-10: The cover is gradually opened ("Roll up little," then "Open
half"). This is a process called hardening off, where the plant is slowly
introduced to lower humidity and more air circulation to prevent shock
when the cover is fully removed.
- Day 11: "Remove" the plastic cover entirely, as the graft is considered
strong enough to survive in the open air.

### PDF Page 82

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=82

3. Shading
- Days 0-8: "Dark (double mesh)" or "Dark (single mesh)" shows that the
seedlings need to be heavily shaded. This reduces the rate of
photosynthesis and water loss from the leaves, preventing wilting while
the vascular connection is weak.
- Days 9-11: "Open (morning only)" or continued reduced shading indicates
a gradual increase in light exposure. This final step of hardening off
prepares the plant for full sunlight without causing sunburn or stress.

Temperature control.
During the first several days after grafting, the healing chamber should be completely
enclosed with plastic sheets to maintain high humidity. However, this setup can cause the
internal aid temperature to rice excessively. To keep the temperature lower than 28 °C,
the chamber should be covered with black shade net.

After a few days, gradually reduce the shading layers from 2 to 3 until they are eventually
removed when the chamber is ready to be opened. It is important to allow the seedlings
to resume photosynthesis during the healing process. Prolonged shading can hinder
photosynthetic activity and slow down seedling growth and recovery.

Important Precautions and Risks
While misting is necessary, over-misting or incorrect spraying can be detrimental to the
healing process. The main risks include:

- Fungal and Bacterial Diseases: Constant moisture on the leaves and stem can
create an ideal environment for diseases like Botrytis (gray mold) and other
fungal or bacterial infections. This is particularly dangerous if a pathogen enters
the fresh wound of the graft union.
- Waterlogging the Soil: Excessive misting can saturate the potting mix, leading to
root rot in the rootstock, which would compromise the health of the entire
seedlings.
- Failed Graft Union: A heavy spray can physically dislodge a still-fragile graft
union, causing it to fail. Excess water can also interfere with the formation of the
callus tissue that holds the two parts together.

The key to successful misting is to prioritize maintaining a high-humidity environment
within the healing chamber while keeping the seedlings and their growing medium from
becoming excessively wet. The goal is to provide just enough moisture to prevent wilting
without creating conditions that encourage disease or damage the graft.

D. Keys to Successful Grafting

1. Cleanliness is Paramount. Always use sterile tools and materials to prevent
the transfer of pathogens.
2. Matching Stem Diameters. Ensure that the scion and rootstock have similar
stem diameters to achieve a proper fit and form a strong graft union.
3. Precise and Quick Cuts. Perform a single, clean cut and immediately join the
scion and rootstock to minimize tissue dehydration.
4. Optimal Environment. High humidity and controlled temperature inside the
healing chamber are essential for a successful graft union.
5. Proper Timing. Conduct grafting when the plants are young and actively
growing for best results.
6. Select a suitable rootstock variety. Choose a rootstock with high resistance
to bacterial wilt, fusarium wilt, verticillium wilt and nematodes. (In MV2C
project, “Suketto” from Kaneko Seeds was used.)
7. Moisten the Healing Chamber Floor. If the chamber floor is dry, apply water
before placing the grafted seedlings inside to maintain humidity.
8. Graft during cooler periods of the day. Perform grafting early in the morning
or late afternoon when sunlight is less intense to reduce plant stress.

E. Cautions When Planting Grafted Tomatoes

- Keep the Graft Union Above the Soil. This is the most critical rule. If the scion's
tissue comes into contact with the soil, it may develop its own roots, defeating
the purpose of the disease-resistant rootstock.
- Careful Handling. Handle the grafted seedlings gently during transplanting to
avoid damaging the new and still-fragile graft union.

Figure 22 shows that the graft union must be positioned above the soil surface when
planted. If the graft union is planted under the soil, the scion may develop its own roots,
making the plant susceptible to the same soil-borne diseases that the resistant rootstock
is meant to protect against.

### PDF Page 85

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=85

Additionally, any adventitious roots emerging from the scion should be removed by hand
to ensure that the plant remains fully dependent on the rootstock.

Figure 22. Transplanting Depth

The rootstock may be cut either above or below the cotyledons depending on the desired
outcome. Cutting above the cotyledons provide greater distance between the graft union
and the soil surface, reducing the likelihood of adventitious root development from the
scion. However, this method may lead to rootstock regrowth, as the remaining meristem
tissue can produce unwanted suckers.

Conversely, cutting the rootstock below the cotyledons eliminates the risk of sucker
formation, since all meristematic tissue is removed. Regardless of the method used, it is
crucial to ensure during transplanting that the graft union remains above the soil surface
to maintain the effectiveness of the graft.

Summary

In summary, adherence to the guidelines provided will enable practitioners to perform
tomato grafting effectively, resulting in healthier plants, increased yields, and a more
sustainable production system. This practice is particularly important for long-term
tomato cultivation, as it enhances plant resistance to soil-borne diseases and
environmental stresses.

Mastery of tomato grafting requires consistent practice, precision, and attention to detail.
Through diligent application of the techniques discussed, practitioners can develop the
necessary competence to perform successful grafting and contribute to the improvement
of sustainable tomato production.

Title: The Legacy of a Grafted Tomato
Time Allotment: 5 minutes

Procedure:
1. Introduction (1 minute): Hold up the tomato. "We've spent our time
today learning about the science and practice of grafting. We've talked
about scions, rootstocks, and how we bring them together. But what is
the ultimate result of all that effort? It's this."
2. The Demonstration (2 minutes):
- Slowly and deliberately, cut the tomato in half.

to resist disease and absorb nutrients, and the stem of the other
plant gave it the ability to produce this delicious fruit.
3. The Sharing (1 minute):
- Carefully slice the tomato and offer a small piece to a few

about the union of the scion and the rootstock?

This activity brings the lesson to life. Cutting and sharing the tomato shows that
grafting isn't just an idea—it's a practical method that creates real, high-quality results.

Statement to end the Lesson:

Your knowledge of grafting now represents a powerful tool for understanding
innovation and collaboration in agriculture. Just like the tomato, your new skills are a
result of two ideas coming together to create something better.

Lesson 4

Tomato Cultivation Method for Long Term Harvesting

This lesson discusses the principles and practices of cultivating tomatoes for extended and
continuous harvests using facility-based system such as greenhouses, high tunnels, and
protective structures. Facility cultivation allows growers to control environment
conditions, optimize plant health, and produce high quality fruits year-round.

Lesson Objective
At the end of the lesson, the participants should be able to design and manage a
tomato cultivation system that support sustainable high yield production.

Specifically, the participants should be able to:
1. explain the advantages of facility-based tomato cultivation of indeterminate
types for long term harvesting;
2. describe the step-by-step cultivation process from nursery preparation to
transplanting, management, and harvesting; and
3. demonstrate proper techniques for pruning, and trellising

Lesson Proper

A. Introduction

Tomato (Lycopersicon esculentum Mill) or kamatis originated from the Andes region
of South America, and is a widely cultivated crop in the Philippines and worldwide. It
is a common ingredient in Philippine dishes. Tomatoes can also be eaten raw, in
salads, or processed into paste or sauces. Tomatoes are known to have carotene and
lycopene. Both are antioxidants that help prevent cancer. It is also a good source of
vitamin C.

In low-elevation areas in Luzon, tomatoes are usually planted from October to March
when the weather is cool and the climate is dry. Planting is done in slightly elevated
areas such as Laguna and Quezon from January to February. Certain areas in Laguna,
Quezon, Batangas, Nueva Ecija, Bukidnon, and Misamis Oriental, grow tomatoes
during the wet season to take advantage of the low supply.

In the Philippines, it plays a vital role in both household consumption and
agribusiness, with increasing demand for year-round supply. Traditional open-field
cultivation often limits harvest to a short window, but long-term harvesting through
protected cultivation offers a sustainable and profitable alternative, and it is suitable
in cool area, such as Benguet Ptovince.
.
Protected cultivation is growing tomatoes inside a controlled environment like
greenhouses, net houses, or tunnels. These structures shield crops from harsh
weather, pests, and diseases—creating ideal conditions for growth and yield.

Being able to ship tomatoes for a long-term can minimize the impact of volatile
market fluctuation. Thus, it can contribute to improvement and constant income for
small-scale vegetable growers.

B. Tomato Varieties

Tomato varieties are generally classified into two main types: determinate and
indeterminate. Diamante Max, one of the most popular varieties in the Philippines, is
a semi-determinate type and is one of the determinate types. Most cherry tomato
varieties, on the other hand, are indeterminate.

Indeterminate tomato plants can continue growing and producing new flowers and
fruits indefinitely, as long as conditions such as temperature, water, fertilizer and pest
and disease management are well maintained. This prolonged growth is possible
because tomato plants do not respond to day length. In the other words, only
indeterminate varieties can produce a very long-term harvest.

1. Indeterminate Varieties

Indeterminate varieties are ideal for long-term harvesting in protected
cultivation (e.g., greenhouses), as they continue to grow and produce fruit over
time. Cherry tomato varieties are indeterminate type. Table 7 shows the different
indeterminate varieties of tomato.

2. Determinate Varieties

Determinate varieties are better suited for open-field or short-cycle production
due to their compact growth and synchronized fruiting. They are not typically
intended for long-term harvests. Some determinate varieties, however, may also
perform well in greenhouse conditions. For example, Ranger was confirmed
through the MV2C project to perform well under greenhouse cultivation. Table 8
are examples of determinate varieties.

The figure below (Figure 23) explains the difference between determinate type
and indeterminate type of tomato.

Determinate or semi-determinate type
- Most commercial tomato varieties in the Philippines are semi-
determinate or determinate types.
- The main stem of these plants eventually stops growing on its own, a
process known as self-pinching.

Indeterminate type
- Most of the salad type/American type/Beef type tomatoes, as well as
cherry tomato varieties, are indeterminate.
- The main stem continues to grow as long as environment conditions
are favorable.
- Long-term harvest is possible with this type
- Tomatoes are not photoperiod sensitive, they do not depend on day
length for growth or flowering.

Figure 23. Tomato type and plant behavior.

C. Cultivation Methods

The cultivation methods of indeterminate type of tomato plants for long-term harvest are
discussed below.

1. Seedling Production

Using grafted seedlings to prevent soil-borne diseases in greenhouse cultivation
is strongly recommended. For details on grafted seedling production, refer to
Lesson 3: Grafting of Tomato Seedlings.

About 250g of seed (approximately 70,000 seeds) are required to produce
enough seedlings to plant one hectare of an indeterminate variety, while 125g of
seed is sufficient for a determinate variety.

Sow the seeds at 0.5 cm deep. Seedlings will emerge within 8 days under optimal
soil temperatures of 20–30°C.

### PDF Page 96

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=96

Seedlings raised in trays with individual cells are generally healthier and more
vigorous than those grown in flats or seedbeds, as the latter may suffer root
damage when the plants are separated for transplanting.

When using cell trays, seedlings are usually transplanted to the main field 30-45
days after sowing. When using plastic pots, seedlings can be kept for up to 60
days before transplanting – a conventional practice previously common in Japan.

There are different methods of seedling production. Figure 24 below shows the
three (3) main methods – cell tray, open field and pot seedlings.

Figure 24. Raising seedling methods for tomato.

2. Land Preparation

Proper land preparation is essential for successful tomato cultivation.

Field Layout
Determinate or semi-determinate and indeterminate tomato varieties require
different field lay-outs. Determinate types tend to grow more horizontally, while
indeterminate types grow vertically. Consequently, the planting density for
indeterminate varieties is usually higher than that for determinate types.

Figure 25 illustrates an example of a field layout for indeterminate-type tomato
plants, which are typically planted in two rows per planting bed.

Fertilizer Application Rate
Tomato plants can exhibit excessive vegetative growth when too much Nitrogen
is applied. Therefore, it is recommended to apply only a minimal amount of
fertilizer before planting and to adjust soil nutrients through top-dressing during
the reproductive phase.

Top-dressing should be applied every two weeks after the first fruit cluster has
set. Table 9 shows the nutrient requirements and standard fertilizer application
rates. The rate of basal fertilizer application should be adjusted based on soil
analysis results to ensure optimal nutrient balance.

Field Preparation and Fertilizer Application Method
The soil should be plowed manually or two to three times using a tractor to a
depth of 20-30 cm, followed by proper leveling. Create furrows with one meter
distance.

It is recommended to apply half of the processed chicken manure (PCM) and
chemical fertilizer in the ditch at the center of the planting bed, and the
remaining half on the surface. This allows plant roots to access the nutrients as
they grow, particularly during the fruit development stage, while preventing
excessive vegetative growth caused by too much surface-applied fertilizer (see
the figure below).

Tips for Tomato Field Preparation
- Planting bed: Prepare high beds to ensure good drainage.
- Fertilizer placement: Apply half of the PCM/ compost and basal
fertilizer in the center of the bed.
- Fertilizer Amount: Avoid applying too much basal fertilizer,
especially nitrogen. Manage plant growth through top-dressing
instead.

The following figure illustrates the proper method of basal fertilizer application
and planting bed preparation.

Figure 26. Method of basal fertilizer application and preparation of planting beds.

3. Transplanting

Transplant seedlings 50 cm apart with 1 meter between rows. After
transplanting, press the soil gently around the base of each seedling and water
immediately. Replace any missing hills 5-7 days after transplanting.

To conserve soil moisture and suppress weed growth, cover the soil with rice
straw or plastic mulch. Avoid planting seedlings too deeply, as this increases the
risk of soil-borne diseases.

The following figure illustrates proper transplanting methods and helpful tips.

### PDF Page 99

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=99

Figure 27. Tips in transplanting tomato seedlings.

4. Plant Management

Trellising
A trellis is a structure built to support the vertical growth of tomato plants. It is
commonly made from bamboo, ipil-ipil poles or plastic and iron posts. This is
done after transplanting by tying the main stems to the support poles and
training them upward using plastic strings.

Trellising is essential for indeterminate tomato varieties, as it helps support
plant growth, improves air circulation, and prevents fruits from touching the soil,
thereby reducing the risk of disease and fruit damage.

Figure 28. Tying the main stem of indeterminate tomato variety to the poles (left).
Indeterminate tomato plants tied to the poles in an open field (right).

Removing side shoots and training the plant
The method of training tomato plants differs depending on the plant type. For
indeterminate varieties, the common practice is to remove all side shoots,
maintaining only the main stem – a technique known as one-stem training. When
removing side shoots, it is important to ensure that hands or tools used are clean.
Scissors should be disinfected with 70% alcohol before use to prevent the spread
of disease.

### PDF Page 100

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=100

In the two-stem training method, the side shoot located just below the first fruit
cluster is retained and developed as the second stem, as it is typically the
strongest side shoot on the plant.

The following figure shows one-stem training method and its tips.

Figure 29. One-stem training method for indeterminate type of tomato plants.

Irrigation

During the vegetative growth stage, one has to be careful not to over-irrigate.
Excessive watering can cause elongation of tomato plants and increase the risk
of disease development.

The frequency of irrigation depends on weather conditions and soil type.
During the fruiting stage, water the plants once a week and reduce irrigation to
once every 10 days during the harvesting stage.

If daily irrigation is possible, apply approximately 1 liter of water per plant per
day during the reproductive stage, adjusting the amount according to weather
conditions – particularly on sunny days.

Covering the soil with rice straw or plastic mulch helps conserve soil moisture.

Top-dressing application of fertilizer
It is recommended to start top-dressing fertilizer application when the first fruit
set of the first cluster is confirmed and the fruits reach approximately the size of
a 1-peso coin. After this stage, top-dressing should be applied every two weeks.
The recommended fertilizer amounts are provided in Table 9. Nutrient
Requirements and Standard Fertilizer Application Rates.

Ensuring Proper Fruit set
Although a tomato flower contain both male and female organs and are naturally
self-pollinating, vibrations greatly enhance pollination efficiency. In greenhouse
conditions, there is little wind and few pollinating insects, manual methods such
as tapping the plants or support poles can help improve pollination. In Japan, a

### PDF Page 101

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=101

fruit-set hormone called “Tomato Tone” is commonly used to enhance fruit set.
The following figure explains methods to ensure proper fruit set.

Additionally, tomato fruit-set is sensitive to high temperatures. When the
temperature is higher than about 30 ℃, the growth of the pollen tube is
suppressed, preventing it from reaching the ovule (Peet et al., 1997). This can
result in poor fruit-set and consequently lower yield.

Figure 30. How to ensure the fruit set of tomato.

Thinning of Fruits
Thinning tomato fruits helps improve fruit size, uniformity and the distribution
of nutrients within the plant. The number of fruits per cluster is usually limited
to four to five to ensure better fruit development and quality.

The following figure shows methods of thinning fruits and pinching the growing
point of the main stem in indeterminate tomato plants.

### PDF Page 102

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=102

Figure 31. Methods of thinning fruits and pinching the growing point of the main stem.

D. Harvesting

The first harvest usually starts 50-60 days from transplanting or approximately 55-
60 days after flowering. Harvesting can be done 2-3 times per week.

The stage of maturity at harvest depends on the season and distance to the market.
For long-distance markets, fruits should be harvested at the mature green stage. For
local markets, fruits are harvested at the breaker stage – when the peel shows a slight
tinge of orange or red – is recommended.

In general, tomato fruits can be harvested at breaker or turning (see the figure below).
Harvesting earlier that this stage may result in fruits that fail to develop full red
coloration.

The best flavor is achieved when fruits are harvested at the red ripe state, though
fruits at this stage are more susceptible to postharvest losses.

After harvesting, place the fruits in plastic or wooden crates lined with banana leaves
or used newspaper to minimize mechanical damage. Bruised and damaged fruits
should be removed immediately, and fruits of similar maturity should be packed
together in the same container.

Figure 32. Harvesting stage of tomato fruits. Breaker (left) and Turning stage (right).

MV2C project

Summary

In summary, this lesson provided an overview of tomato production, covering variety
selection, cultivation, and harvesting. Tomatoes are classified into determinate, semi-
determinate, and indeterminate types, each suited to different production systems.
Successful cultivation involves using healthy or grafted seedlings, proper land preparation,
balanced fertilization, and appropriate irrigation. Practices such as trellising, training, and
fruit thinning help manage plant growth and improve yield and quality. Pollination may be
enhanced through vibration or hormone application, especially in greenhouses.
Harvesting begins about 50–60 days after transplanting, with the maturity stage
depending on market distance—mature green for distant transport and breaker to red
ripe for local markets—to ensure quality and reduce postharvest losses.

Lesson 5

Sweet Pepper Cultivation Method for Long Term
Harvesting

This lesson introduces the complete method of cultivating sweet peppers (Capsicum
annuum L.) with a focus on sustainable, long-term harvesting techniques. Sweet
peppers—also known as bell peppers—are a valuable crop grown worldwide for their
versatility, nutritional value, and profitability.

Lesson Objective
At the end of the lesson, the participants should be able to demonstrate proper
cultivation of sweet pepper in a protected facility to increase yield and extend
production.

Specifically, the participants should be able to:
1. identify suitable sweet pepper varieties based on local climate, soil conditions,
and market demand;
2. prepare and manage a seedling nursery, including proper media preparation,
sowing, watering, and hardening;
3. prepare land or container systems for transplanting, using appropriate spacing,
soil amendments, and mulching;
4. transplant seedlings correctly to ensure high survival and early growth;
5. apply effective irrigation and fertilization practices throughout the growing
period to support healthy plant development;
6. implement techniques for long-term harvesting, such as staking, pruning, and
training where needed; and
7. harvest sweet peppers properly and at the right maturity stage to ensure good
market quality.

Time Allotment: 4 hours
Methodologies: Lecture and Field Demonstration
Tools to Use: Laptop, LCD projector, PowerPoint (PPT) presentation and
demonstration materials

For the demonstration: seeds, seedlings, fertilizer, agro-chemicals,
strings

A. Introduction
B. Variety of Sweet Pepper
C. Cultivation Methods
D. Harvesting

Procedure
1. Begin with a light, friendly tone: “Before we dive into sweet pepper
cultivation, let’s see — if you were a plant, what kind would you be? Each
plant grows differently, just like each of us has our own way of growing and
thriving.
2. Ask participants to think about which plant best represents their personality.
Give a few examples:
Cactus – Strong, independent, can survive tough conditions.
Flower – Colorful, delicate, needs care and attention to bloom.
Fruit Tree – Patient, takes time to grow but produces lasting results.
Vine – Flexible, grows fast, but needs support to climb.
3. Encourage them to share their choice and explain why.

Key Concepts/Messages:
- Every plant species has unique needs and growth habits.
- Understanding the “personality” of the crop — like sweet pepper — helps in
applying the right cultivation practices.
- Successful long-term harvesting depends on matching your management
style to the plant’s natural behavior.

Connecting statement to the lesson:

“Just like us, plants have their own personalities — different needs, strengths, and
sensitivities. Some need more water, others less sunlight. Sweet pepper has its own
‘personality’ too. It’s sensitive to water shortage, requires balance in fertilization, and
grows best when trained properly. Today, we’ll learn how to understand and manage
that personality — to help it grow productively for a long time.”

Lesson Proper

A. Introduction

Sweet pepper (Capsicum annuum L.), also known as 'bell pepper', originated from
central and south America, and belongs to Solanaceae family. It is usually an annual
crop but in tropics it becomes perennial. It has several types of fruits, e.g. bell type,
conical type, with various size and colors. It is also referred to by other names such as
capsicum, pepper, chili, or paprika. Sweet peppers are rich in essential nutrients,
particularly vitamins A and C, as well as potassium (Mariano & Jimenez, 2021).

In the Philippines, sweet pepper production has shown a positive trend from 2019 to
2021. Production levels ranged from 13.95 thousand metric tons to 15.96 thousand
metric tons, with an average annual increase of 7.0% over the three-year period (PSA,
2021). On a per capita basis, the average net food disposable for sweet pepper is only
0.13 kilograms per year, with an average growth rate of 4.7% (Tumbaga and Valler,
2025).

1. Climate and Soil Requirements

Sweet peppers grow best on temperatures between 21 and 24°C. Growth and
yields decrease when temperatures drop below 18°C or rise above 27°C for
prolonged periods. Sweet peppers can tolerate daytime temperatures over 30°C,
provided that night temperatures remain within the optimal range of 21–24°C.

These crops are not sensitive to photoperiod or humidity, meaning that day
length and relative humidity do not significantly affect flowering or fruit set. They
grow best in a loam or silty-loam soils with good water-holding capacity but can
also grow on other soil types, as long as the soil is well drained. The ideal soil pH
ranges from 5.5 and 6.8.

2. Characteristics of Sweet Pepper

Sweet pepper is an erect, branched, herbaceous annual plant characterized by a
shallow taproot system. The stems are green and become slightly woody with
age. The leaves are simple, alternate, ovate to lanceolate with entire margins. The
flowers are solitary, axillary, white to greenish, actinomorphic and bisexual. The
fruit is a large, fleshy berry that is globose to blocky in shape, green when
immature and turning red, yellow, or orange at maturity. The seeds are
numerous, small, flat, and yellowish-white, embedded in a spongy central
placenta.

Table 10 below shows the growth stages of sweet pepper plants.

B. Variety of Sweet Pepper

Almost all the commercial varieties of sweet peppers are indeterminate types, unlike
varieties of tomato. This means that, under favorable environmental conditions, the
plants can continue growing for a long period since they are insensitive to day length.

The variety ‘California Wonder’ is one of the oldest and most popular bell-type
varieties, originally developed in the United States in 1828. The followings are
examples of sweet pepper varieties. Where color is not specified, green fruits turn red
upon ripening.

a) California Wonder – bell type – Open pollinated (OP)
b) Yolo Wonder – bell type – OP
c) Green 500 – conical type –F1- Hybrid (F1)
d) Rain Hardy – bell type –F1

C. Cultivation Methods

1. Seedling Production
Things to consider in nursery establishment:
- The nursery must be located near a reliable source of water.
- It should be located at least 20 meters away from other pepper, tomato and
eggplant to prevent the transmission of diseases to the seedlings.
- Good sanitation must be always practiced. All plant debris and trash should
be burned between production cycles to reduce the risk of pest and disease
buildup.

Refer to Lesson 4: Tomato Cultivation Method for Long Term Harvesting for detailed
procedures on raising seedlings. The use of cell trays or vinyl pots is recommended
for producing healthy and uniform sweet pepper seedlings.

2. Land Preparation
a. Field layout
For long-term harvest of sweet pepper, the plants need wider space than the
usual cultivation. The standard planting distances for 4-branches
cultivation to achieve long-term harvest are as follows and also illustrated
on Figure 34:
- Bed width = 1.0m
- Distance between beds = 0.5m, 1 row/bed,
- Distance between plants = 0.5 m. (makes 13,333 plants/ha)
- Bed height = 0.2 m. The high planting bed is recommended for
good drainage.

The sweet pepper plant is not highly sensitive to fertilizer application unlike
tomato plants, which tend to grow excessively when too much Nitrogen is
applied. However, the proper application of basal fertilizer is still important
and should be supplemented with top-dressing during the growth period as
needed.

The standard fertilizer application rate is presented in Table 11, which

After forming the plots, it is recommended to apply half of the processed

nutrients gradually, particularly during the fruit-enlargement stage when
nutrient demand is highest.

3. Transplanting
Wait until the seedlings have 2-4 true leaves and strong stems before
transplanting. Refer to Lesson 4: Tomato Cultivation Method for Long Term
Harvesting for detailed transplanting procedures. Seedlings should not be
planted too deep to minimize the risk of soil-borne diseases.

Choose a cloudy day or late afternoon for transplanting to reduce plant stress.
Water the soil thoroughly after transplanting to help the roots establish well in
their new environment.

4. Plant Management
a. Training the plants
The four-branch training method is recommended for long-term harvesting
of sweet pepper. In this method, the first flower, as well as dense or
excessively elongated branches, are usually removed or pruned to promote
balanced growth. The four main branches are pinched at around 170 cm to
control plant height and encourage fruit development.

When removing branches or pinching the growing points of the main
branches, it is important to ensure that hands and pruning tools are clean.
Scissors should be disinfected by 70% alcohol before use to prevent disease
transmission. Figure 37 illustrates the management of the four-branch
training method.

b. Irrigation
Sweet pepper plants generally require ample water and are sensitive to
water shortages due to their shallow root system. It is recommended to
saturate the field once before transplanting to ensure sufficient soil
moisture during seedling establishment.

Throughout the growing period, Sweet pepper needs a regular and
moderate water supply, with irrigation being most critical during flowering
and fruit setting stages. Irrigation is applied every 7–10 days in light soils
and every 10–12 days in heavy soils, preferably using furrow or drip
irrigation methods. However, waterlogging must be avoided to prevent root
diseases and fruit drop.

For greenhouse cultivation, drip irrigation is recommended, as it ensures
efficient water use, maintains optimal soil moisture, and reduces disease
risk.

Occasional sprinkler irrigation is also recommended to prevent pest
buildup. Therefore, a combination of over-plant (sprinkler) and drip
irrigation is suggested for best results.

c. Top-dressing application of fertilizer
Top-dressing should be applied every two weeks, starting from the fruit-
enlargement stage of the first fruit or the second fruit (if the first fruit is
removed). The recommended amount of fertilizer is presented in Table 11:
Nutrient Requirement and Recommended Application Rate.

D. Harvesting
Sweet peppers should be harvested when fruits reach full size and become firm, but
before they begin to change color, unless harvesting for mature colored fruits (yellow,
orange, or red).

The period from flowering to optimum harvest takes 35–40 days, although this may
vary depending on the variety, desired fruit color and environmental conditions. As

### PDF Page 117

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=117

the stems of pepper plants are fragile, fruits should be harvested using a knife or
pruning shears to avoid damaging the plant.

Postharvest handling of sweet pepper involves careful harvesting, cleaning, and
grading, followed by storage at 7–10 °C with high humidity. Fruits should be packed
in ventilated containers and handled gently during transport to maintain freshness
and extend shelf life.

Summary

In summary, this lesson provided essential practices for successful and sustained sweet
pepper production. It introduces the crop’s growth characteristics and environmental
requirements, highlights commonly used indeterminate commercial varieties suited for
extended harvests, and details the cultivation methods—including seedling production,
land preparation, transplanting and harvesting—to ensure healthy plant growth and
continuous fruiting. Also, proper harvesting techniques and postharvest handling are
important to maintain fruit quality, extend shelf life, and maximize yield over a prolonged
production period.

Lesson 6

Plant Nutrition Diagnosis

This lesson introduces how to diagnose nutrition status of vegetable crops. It also provides
basic knowledge on how different nutrients move in the vascular system of the plant.

Lesson Objective
At the end of the lesson, the participants should be able to diagnose nutrition
status by visual observations in the farm.

Specifically, the participants should be able to:
1. describe the function and importance of each nutrients;
2. recognize the nutritional status of vegetable plants by field observations;
3. demonstrate proper application of top-dressing fertilizer during plants’ growth;
and
4. compute for the fertilizer application rate for the next season.

Time Allotment: 4 hours
Methodologies: Lecture-discussion and Farm Demonstration
Tools to Use: Laptop, LCD projector, PowerPoint (PPT) presentation

CONTENTS
A. Introduction: Why is Diagnosis of Nutrient Deficiency Important?
B. Plant Nutrients
C. Plant Nutrient Mobility
D. Key to Visual Diagnosis of Nutrient Deficiency
E. Typical Symptoms of Nutrient Deficiency and Excess

Quiz 2:What is the common name of this problem on the tomato fruit? (hint:

2. Explain the correct answer, the reason and key concepts in order to

Quiz 1: The correct answer is "d" (frost injury). An important point to note is that the
damage is quite uniform throughout the field. Most environmentally induced problems
tend to be uniform, whereas parasitic diseases may begin as spots throughout the field.
Of course, you can check the weather and see that frost did indeed occur just prior to
the widespread appearance of this problem.

Quiz 2: The correct answer is "b". Fruit exposed to long periods of bright, hot sunlight
may show "scalded", shriveled, and dried tissue, known as "sunscald" or sometimes
"sunburn". It appears only on the side of fruit facing to the outside of the canopy, where
the tissue is exposed to the ravages of the sun.

Lesson Proper

A. Introduction: Why is Diagnosis of Nutrient Deficiency Important?

Soil fertility management based on the status of soil nutrients is one of the most
critical factors for successful vegetable production. However, soil analysis through
laboratory testing can be time consuming and costly. In addition, there are limitations
to soil diagnosis based solely on chemical analysis results, as these can vary
depending on the soil sampling location and the analytical method used.

For long-term harvest cultivation of fruit vegetables such as tomato and sweet pepper,
proper soil fertility management through periodic top-dressing over several months
is essential. Therefore, being able to visually assess the nutritional status of plants is
a valuable skill for growers.

Visual diagnosis of nutrient deficiency for plants is important because of the following
reasons:
- Soil testing laboratories or soil test kits are not always available.
- Laboratory results often take time, which may delay timely fertilizer
application.
- Managing the nutritional status of fruit vegetables is especially important in
long-term harvesting systems.
- The ability to distinguish nutrient imbalance symptoms from disease or
physiological disorders is very helpful in the field.
- Results of soil chemical analysis can vary depending on sampling techniques
and analytical methods.

Figure 39 below shows that plants have different types of root systems, which
influence their nutrient absorption and response to fertilization.

Figure 39. Different root systems of different plants
