B. Plant Nutrients
It is necessary to know what elements/nutrients are needed for plant growth.

a. Essential plant nutrients
Sixteen (16) chemical nutrients are known to be important for plants’ growth.
They are called as Essential Plant Nutrients. The 16 elements are divided into
two main groups:
- Non-mineral elements: Plants get these from air and water. These are:
Hydrogen (H), Oxygen (O), Carbon (C)
- Mineral elements/nutrients: Plants uptake these from the soil. These are:
Nitrogen (N), Phosphorus (P), Potassium (K), Calcium (Ca), Magnesium
(Mg), Sulfur (S), Boron (B), Cupper (Cu), Iron (Fe), Chloride (Cl), Manganese
(Mn), Molybdenum (Mo), Zinc (Zn)

Additionally, Nickel (Ni) is recently found to be one of the essential elements for
plants.

b. Mineral nutrients
The thirteen (13) mineral nutrients are categorized in two major groups, i.e.
macronutrients and micronutrients.
- Macronutrients
o Primary nutrients: N, P, K
o Secondary nutrients: Ca, Mg, S
- Micronutrients
o B, Cu, Fe, Cl, Mn, Mo, Zn

The primary nutrients are known as the most important nutrients for plant
growth, and they are usually added to the soil by chemical fertilizer. The diagram
below shows a summary of their major roles.

- Makes protein and becomes the basis Nitrogen
of chlorophyll
(N)
- Develop leaves and branches

Phosphorus • Basis of cell formation at growing point
(P) • Regulates flowering and fruiting

- Promotes sap flow Potassium
- Balances growth of each part (K)
- Enhances growth of root

Figure 40. Major role of primary nutrients

### PDF Page 128

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=128

A more detailed explanation of the role of N, P and K is provided below:

Nitrogen (N)
- Nitrogen is an important element found in all living cells.
- It is a key part of proteins, enzymes and other substances that help plants make
and use energy.
- It is also a component of chlorophyll, the green pigment that allows plants to
carry out photosynthesis.
- Helps plants grow quickly, produce more seeds and fruits and improve the
quality of leaves and forage.
- Plants get Nitrogen mainly from fertilizers and from the air through Nitrogen
fixation by Rhizobium bacteria found in legume roots.

Phosphorus (P)
- Phosphorous is an essential element involved in the process of photosynthesis.
- It plays a key role in the formation of oils, sugars, and starches in plants.
- Helps transform solar energy into chemical energy; supports proper plant
maturation; and improves the plant’s ability to withstand stress.
- It promotes rapid growth, encourages flowering (blooming), and strengthens
root development
- Common sources of phosphorous include fertilizers, bone meal, and phosphate
rocks.

Potassium (K)
- Potassium is absorbed by plants in large amounts – second only to Nitrogen,
and in some cases, Calcium (Ca).
- It is essential for the movement of sugars and nutrients through the phloem.
- Helps transport photosynthates (such as sucrose) from the leaves to storage
organs like roots, fruits, and seeds.
- It supports the formation of proteins, enhances photosynthesis, improves fruit
quality and helps reduce disease incidence.
- Potassium also regulates the opening and closing of stomata, helping control
water loss through transpiration.
- It is supplied to plants through soil minerals, organic matter, and fertilizers.

C. Plant Nutrient Mobility
When conducting visual diagnosis of nutrient deficiency in the field, it is important to
understand the mobility of each nutrient within the plant.

Mobile nutrients can move relatively freely through the plant’s vascular system,
allowing them to be redistributed from older tissues to younger, actively growing
parts where they are most needed. As a result, the deficiency symptoms of mobile
nutrients appear first in the older leaves or mature parts of the plant.

In contrast, immobile nutrients cannot move easily within the plant once they are
deposited in certain tissues. Therefore, they cannot reach the actively growing areas
when a deficiency occurs, and symptoms appear on the younger leaves or newly
developed parts of the plant.

There are intermediate nutrients, whose mobility depends on various physiological
and environmental factors. For these nutrients, visual diagnosis can be more

### PDF Page 129

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=129

challenging, as their deficiency symptoms may appear inconsistently across different
plant parts.

Mobility of nutrients in plant body
Mobile nutrients: N, P, K
Immobile nutrients: Ca, Fe, B
Intermediate: S, Mg, Cl, Cu, Zn, Mn, Mo

application of a top-dressing fertilizer is needed. However, it is important to
remember that environmental conditions – such as soil type, temperature, and
moisture – can influence plant responses. Therefore, the chart may need to be
adjusted under certain conditions.

E. Typical Symptoms of Nutrient Deficiency and Excess

The photos below show typical symptoms of nutrient deficiency and excess. They are
mostly pictures of tomato plants which needs sustainable and proper fertilizer
management to maintain plant health and productivity.

- Chlorosis – This condition occurs when plant leaves produce insufficient
chlorophyll, causing the leaf tissue to turn yellow.
- Necrosis – This refers to the death of plant tissue, which appears as brown
or black spots on leaves, stems, or roots. Necrosis is the result of irreversible
cell damage in the affected areas.

1. Symptom of nutrient deficiency
Nitrogen (N) deficiency
Nitrogen deficiency symptoms first appear on the older leaves, which develop
chlorosis or yellowing. The affected leaves usually turn uniformly yellow, and a
reddish coloration may be observed along the veins and petioles. Meanwhile, the
younger leaves at the top remain green but appear paler than normal. The upper
leaves become smaller, and the entire plant exhibits stunted growth because of
insufficient nitrogen needed for protein synthesis and cell development.

Figure 42. Symptoms of nitrogen deficiency.

Phosphorus (P) deficiency
Plants suffering from Phosphorous deficiency often become dwarfed or stunted.
In some crops such as tomato, lettuce and the brassicas, a characteristic purpling
of the stems, petioles and undersides of the lower leaves may appear.
Phosphorous deficiency symptoms are often difficult to identify.

Figure 43. Symptoms of phosphorous deficiency.

### PDF Page 131

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=131

Potassium (K) deficiency
Potassium deficiency usually appears first on matured leaves, though not always
on the oldest ones. The effected leaves develop interveinal yellowing – yellowing
between the veins. As the deficiency worsens, growth becomes stunted and the
edges and interveinal areas of the leaves turn brown or necrotic. The symptoms
of Potassium deficiency can closely resemble Magnesium deficiency, so careful
diagnosis is necessary.

Figure 44. Symptoms of potassium deficiency

Magnesium (Mg) deficiency
Magnesium deficiency typically appears on matured leaves, but not on the oldest
ones. The main symptom is interveinal chlorosis, where the areas between the
veins becomes pale green or yellow. Although it may resemble Potassium
deficiency, Magnesium deficiency can be distinguished by the patter and location
of chlorosis, which usually starts in the middle of the leaf and progresses
outward.

Figure 45. Symptoms of magnesium deficiency

### PDF Page 132

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=132

Calcium (Ca) deficiency
Calcium deficiency symptoms usually appear at the growing points of plants,
where new tissues are developing. The young leaves often show necrosis around
their bases or margins, and in severe cases, the growing tips may die back.
Common disorders caused by Calcium deficiency include blossom-end rot in
tomatoes and other fruiting vegetables, tip burn in lettuce and black heart in
celery.

Figure 46. Symptoms of calcium deficiency

Iron (Fe) deficiency
Iron deficiency usually shows distinct chlorosis on the younger leaves. The
symptoms can sometime be mistaken for Nitrogen deficiency, which also causes
yellowing; however, Nitrogen deficiency appears first on the lower/older leaves,
while Iron deficiency affects the youngest leaves at the top of the plant.

3. Effect of Soil pH on Availability of Nutrients
The availability of soil nutrients is greatly affected by the soil pH. This means that
plants may be unable to absorb them when the pH is not within the suitable range
even if nutrients are present in sufficient amounts. For example, phosphorus
becomes less available at a low pH (around 5.5) because it tends to become fixed

### PDF Page 135

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=135

in clay minerals, making it difficult for plants to take up. Most nutrients are
readily available when the soil pH is around 6.5, which is why this value is
considered the optimum pH for most crop.

Figure 51. Effects of soil pH on Nutrient Availability to Plants

4. Symptoms of Nutrient Excess
Excess Nitrogen (N) is one of the most common cases of nutrient imbalance.
When Nitrogen levels are too high, the symptoms are:
- Larger leaves than usual size
- Wavy leaves
- Dark green leaves (sometimes brown leaves)
- Thick vines/stems
- Less female flowers with some Cucurbitaceae vegetables
- Malformed fruits

Figure 52. Symptom of Excess Nitrogen in Bitter Gourd (left) and cucumber (right)

### PDF Page 136

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=136

5. Balance of Nutrients
Antagonism. In plant nutrition, maintaining a balance of nutrients is essential
for healthy growth. When one nutrient is present in excessive amount, it can
inhibit the uptake of another nutrient by the plant. This phenomenon is called
antagonism.

Most nutrients are absorbed by plants in the form of ions (for example, K⁺, Ca²⁺,
NO₃⁻). Ions with similar charges or sizes may compete for the same transport
channels or binding sites on the root cell membranes. As a result, when one
nutrient is excessively present, it may suppress the absorption of another,
causing nutrient imbalances or deficiency symptoms – even if the inhibited
nutrient is actually present in sufficient amounts in the soil.

The table below presents some common examples of nutrient antagonism
observed in crop plants.

Table 12. Examples of antagonistic reactions between nutrients.
Excess nutrient Antagonized Nutrient
Ammonium-N Calcium (Ca), Magnesium (Mg), Potassium (K)
(NH4-N)
Nitrate-N (NO3-N) Molybdenum (Mo)
Potassium (K) Magnesium (Mg), Calcium (Ca)
Phosphorus (P) Zinc (Zn), Iron (Fe), Manganese (Mn)

Dilution effect. The dilution effect occurs when plant’s grow rapidly, but the
uptake of certain nutrients cannot catch up with the increased growth rate,
leading to a deficiency of those nutrients.

For example, excessive nitrogen can inhibit the uptake of boron in plants. High
nitrogen levels stimulate vigorous vegetative growth, and if boron absorption
does not increase proportionally, the concentration of boron in plant tissues
becomes diluted. This imbalance can result in boron deficiency.

The pictures below show the typical symptom of boron deficiency in broccoli
(left) and a secondary fungal infection (right) that may have entered through the
damaged plant tissues. These images were taken from a farm in Benguet Province.

Figure 53. Boron Deficiency and Fungal Infection due to Excess Nitrogen Absorption in
Broccoli

Summary

The lesson discussed the symptoms of nutrient deficiency and nutrient excess to help
vegetable growers make informed decisions about fertilizer application rates and to
differentiate nutrient-related symptoms from those caused by physiological disorders,
pests or diseases.

Key Points:
- Daily observation is essential: Regularly monitoring changes in leaf color, shape,
and growth patterns helps identify early signs of imbalances.
- Both deficiency and excess are harmful: Too little or too much of a nutrient can
reduce plant growth, yield and quality.
- Nutrient interactions matter: An excess of one nutrient can inhibit the uptake of
others, leading to secondary deficiencies.
- Soil pH affects nutrient availability: Extreme pH levels can limit the availability
and absorption of essential nutrients.
- Consider environmental and management factors: Proper watering,
temperature control, pest and disease management are also vital for balanced
nutrient uptake and healthy plant growth.

Ender

Title: Plant Doctor Relay
Time Allotment: 10-15 minutes
Materials Needed: Printed photos of plants (tomato and sweet pepper) showing
nutrient deficiencies and excesses

Procedure:
1. Say: “You’ve learned how to identify nutrient deficiencies and excesses.
Now, you’ll become plant doctors! Your task is to diagnose the symptoms
of several ‘patients’ — our plants — and suggest the right treatment.”
2. Explain that each photo represents a plant showing nutrient-related
problems.
3. Set up 4–6 stations around the room or greenhouse, each displaying a
photo or actual sample of a plant with a specific nutrient problem.
4. Each group starts at a different station.
5. Give them 1–2 minutes per station to:
- Observe the symptoms,
- Identify the likely nutrient deficiency or excess, and
- Write their suggested corrective action on the Diagnosis Sheet.
6. When the time is up, blow a whistle or say “Rotate!”
7. Groups move clockwise to the next station until all stations have been
visited.
8. After completing the rotations, gather participants.
9. Review each station’s correct diagnosis and briefly explain the reasoning
(e.g., “Yellowing of lower leaves first — that’s nitrogen deficiency.”).
10. Let groups check their answers and note corrections.

Processing:
1. Ask the participants:
2. Which symptoms were easy to identify? Which were confusing?
3. How can you confirm your diagnosis in the field (besides observation)?
4. Why is it important to avoid over-fertilizing even when symptoms are
unclear?
5. What practices can help prevent nutrient imbalance in your crops?

Key Learning Points:
- Visual observation is a key diagnostic skill.
- Nutrient balance is more important than simply “adding more fertilizer.”
- Field monitoring helps detect early symptoms before yield losses occur.
- Teamwork and experience-sharing improve farmers’ diagnostic
accuracy.

Statement to end the Lesson:
““As farmers, you are the first doctors of your plants. By learning to observe,
diagnose, and respond to plant symptoms early, you not only protect your crops
— you secure your harvest and livelihood.”

SELF-ASSESSMENT

____________1. Why is mobility of nutrients in plant bodies important for diagnosis of
nutrient status of plants?
____________2. What is the typical symptom of phosphorus deficiency?
____________3. What is the typical symptom of potassium deficiency?
____________4. What are the typical symptoms of excess nitrogen of tomato plants?
____________5. What can cause the excess uptake of nitrogen by plants?
____________6. Why is the range of soil pH important?

Answer key:

1. Nutrient mobility within the plant determines the location of deficiency
symptoms.
2. Stunted growth and purple color of lower leaves or stems.
3. Interveinal yellowing of matured leaves (not always the oldest). As the
deficiency progresses, most of the interveinal area become necrotic. It
resembles Mg deficiency.
4. The leaves have dark green color and curl downward.
5. Flower abortion, less female flower in case of some Cucurbitaceae vegetables,
malformed fruits, yield reduction.
6. The range of soil pH can greatly affect nutrient availability to plants.

Lesson 7

Disease Management of Tomato and Sweet Pepper

Sweet pepper (Capsicum annuum L.) and tomato (Solanum lycopersicum L.) are high-
value solanaceous crops widely cultivated in the Philippines. They are key ingredients in
Filipino cuisine and important sources of livelihood for smallholder farmers. However,
productivity is often reduced by fungal, bacterial, viral, and abiotic diseases that thrive in
the country’s tropical climate—characterized by high humidity, fluctuating temperatures,
and seasonal rainfall.

In the Cordillera and other highland areas, cooler temperatures combined with frequent
rains create ideal conditions for disease development. Misdiagnosis, over-reliance on
chemical pesticides, and limited access to clean planting materials further exacerbate
losses.

This lesson will help you correctly identify common pepper and tomato diseases and
implement Integrated Disease Management (IDM) strategies suited to local conditions.

Lesson Objective
At the end of the lesson, the participants should be able to identify tomato and
sweet pepper diseases and to recommend doable management practices.

Specifically, the participants should be able to:
1. define what a plant disease is and describe factors that cause it.
2. distinguish between biotic and abiotic causes of plant disorders.
3. identify common fungal, bacterial, viral, and abiotic diseases of pepper and
tomato.
4. recognize early disease symptoms in the field.
5. apply appropriate Integrated Disease Management (IDM) practices.

Time Allotment: 4 hours
Methodologies: Lecture and Farm visit
Tools to Use: Laptop, LCD projector, PowerPoint (PPT) presentation and
demonstration materials

CONTENTS
A. What is Plant Disease
B. Disease Development (Plant Disease Triangle)
C. Common Tomato and Sweet Pepper Diseases Caused by Pathogens
D. Integrated Disease Management (IDM)

Lesson Proper

A. What is Plant Disease

A plant disease is an abnormal condition in a plant that results from ongoing stress
caused by a living pathogen (Biotic) or environment (Abiotic factor), ultimately
leading to visible symptoms of damage or dysfunction (Agrios, 2005). Let’s discuss
them.

1. Pathogens (Biotic)

Pathogens are living organisms that disrupt a plant’s normal functions, growth,
and development. It can be spread from an infected plant or plant debris to a
healthy plant. Microorganisms that cause plant diseases include nematodes,
fungi, bacteria, and mycoplasmas. We also classify viruses and viroids as biotic
agents because they must have living cells for reproduction and are composed of
nucleic acid and protein.

a. Fungi. Fungi are very small simple plants called molds and depend on other
organisms or plant tissues for food since they do not have chlorophyll. It
multiplies by producing spores which produce threadlike filaments called
hypha that enter the host directly or through natural openings. It can
survive in adverse conditions through special structures (sclerotia) and
infects again when favorable conditions prevail.

Examples: Phytophthora, Alternaria, Colletotrichum

a. Bacteria. Bacteria are small, one-celled organisms that do not have
chlorophyll and multiply through cell division. It infects plants through
wounds or entry points to enter the host. It can survive in soil, plant debris,
seeds or farm tools. Usually spread by wind water, insects, tools or soil.
Symptom is generally rotting of host tissue.

Examples: Xanthomonas, Pseudomonas, Ralstonia

a. Viruses. Viruses are very small organisms, smaller than fungi and bacteria,
and can be seen only under the electron microscope. It is dependent on
living organisms for food and reproduction. Generally, spread by insects
(vectors), seeds, nematodes, fungi, or mechanical methods.

Examples: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus, Pepper Mosaic Virus

a. Nematodes. Nematodes are slender, thread-like, unsegmented worms with
an elongated, cylindrical body. Depending on their food source, they may be
saprophagous (feeding on decaying matter), predaceous (feeding on other
organisms), or plant-parasitic. Plant-parasitic nematodes possess a stylet,
which they use to puncture and feed on plant cells. Their life cycle includes
an egg stage, four larval or juvenile stages, and an adult stage.

Example: Root-knot nematodes

### PDF Page 147

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=147

2. Non-living or Abiotic factors (Environmental/Physiological)
Abiotic factors are non-living conditions in the environment that can cause injury
or disorders in plants. These are often called physiological disorders or non-
infectious diseases because their symptoms may look similar to those caused by
living organisms (like fungi, bacteria, or viruses), but they cannot spread from
one plant to another.

a. Nutrient deficiencies. These are evident through:
- Blossom End Rot – caused by calcium deficiency and irregular watering
- Pale yellow leaves - Nitrogen deficiency
- Marginal leaf scorch and poor fruit quality - Potassium deficiency
- Interveinal chlorosis on older leaves - Magnesium deficiency

b. Nutrient deficiencies. These are evident through:
- Fruit Cracking – due to irregular watering or sudden heavy rain after
drought.
- Blossom End Rot –irregular watering

c. Temperature extremes. These are observed through:
- Catfacing – deformities in fruit caused by cool temperatures during
flowering.
- Sunscald – white or yellow patches on fruit due to excessive sunlight
exposure.
- Chilling Injury – pitting and poor ripening caused by exposure to low
temperatures.

B. Disease Development (Plant Disease Triangle)
Plant disease develops only when three critical factors such as a susceptible host, a
virulent pathogen, and a favorable environment come together at the same time and
place (Figure 1). This interaction is known as the disease triangle, and if any one of
these factors is missing, disease will not occur or will be greatly reduced.

Factors for disease development
1. Host. A host is a plant that can be infected by the pathogen. The host plant should
be susceptible.
Example: Tomato susceptible to Phytophthora infestans (late blight).

2. Pathogen – the pathogen should be virulent and present in high quantities to
cause infection.
Example: Ralstonia solanacearum causes bacterial wilt in tomato and pepper.

3. Environment – Any environmental factor that can cause stress to the plant can
make the plant susceptible (Temperature, relative humidity. …) Example: Cool
and moist condition favors the leaf blight of tomato

Figure 57. Plant Disease Triangle

Factors Favoring Disease Development
- High relative humidity and prolonged leaf wetness
- Monocropping of tomato and pepper
- Lack of crop rotation and sanitation
- Use of infected seeds or seedlings
- Over-irrigation or poorly drained soils
- Inadequate pest control (whiteflies, aphids, thrips)

C. Common Tomato and Sweet Pepper Diseases Caused by Pathogens
Tomatoes and sweet peppers are usually infected by several pathogens, fungi,
bacteria, virus and pest like nematodes causing severe loss if not properly managed.

1. Fungal Diseases
Fungi are the most common pathogens affecting both tomato and pepper,
thriving in humid and wet conditions (Table 1).

2. Bacterial Disease
Bacterial diseases are caused by microscopic single-celled organisms that thrive
in warm, humid conditions and often spread through splashing rain,
contaminated tools, boots, or infected seeds.

Table 14. Bacterial Diseases

Figure 59. Symptoms of Bacterial Diseases in Sweet Pepper

3. Viral Diseases
Viral diseases are caused by very small or microscopic pathogens that cannot live
or reproduce on their own. They are often spread by insect vectors (aphids,
whiteflies, thrips), mechanical transmission (hands, tools), or infected
seeds/transplants.

Table 15. Viral Diseases

Figure 60. Symptoms of Virus Diseases in Sweet Pepper (left) and Tomato (middle and
right)

4. Nematodes
Nematodes are microscopic, worm-like organisms that attack the roots of crops
like tomato and pepper. The most economically important species include root-
knot nematodes (Meloidogyne spp.) and lesion nematodes (Pratylenchus spp.).
Infestation leads to poor plant growth, reduced yield, and increased
susceptibility to other diseases.

5. Abiotic Diseases of Sweet Pepper and Tomato
Abiotic diseases are caused by non-living environmental factors such as nutrient
imbalances, temperature extremes, water stress, and chemical exposure.
Pathogens do not cause these disorders and do not spread from plant to plant.
Proper diagnosis and management are crucial for minimizing yield losses.

D. Integrated Disease Management (IDM)
Integrated Disease Management (IDM) is a comprehensive and preventive strategy
that combines different, complementary methods to manage plant diseases. Its aim is
to keep disease levels low enough to avoid economic loss while reducing excessive
chemical use, promoting both environmental protection and long-term farm
profitability.

1. Cultural Practices
- Use disease-free seeds or certified seedlings
- Use of grafted seedlings for soil-borne diseases
- Crop rotation (avoid planting solanaceous crops successively)
- Field sanitation (removal of infected debris)
- Raised beds and proper drainage
- Mulching and plastic film use in rainy areas
- Proper spacing for ventilation

2. Resistant Varieties
- Use varieties with resistance to Fusarium wilt, TYLCV, or Bacterial wilt.

3. Biological Control
- Use of Trichoderma spp., Bacillus subtilis, Metarrhizium annisopliae (for
vectors)

4. Chemical Control
- Fungicides: Mancozeb, Chlorothalonil, Copper-based
- Bactericides: Streptomycin + copper
- Insecticides: Use of selective insecticides to control vectors (whiteflies,
aphids)

5. Mechanical and Physical Control
- Yellow sticky traps for whiteflies and aphids
- Net houses or low tunnels (protected cultivation)
- Solarization before planting

Summary

This lesson discussed the common diseases affecting sweet pepper and tomato and
teaches farmers how to correctly diagnose and manage them. Diseases in these crops
are caused by biotic agents—fungi, bacteria, viruses, and nematodes—or abiotic factors
such as nutrient deficiencies, water stress, and temperature extremes.

It also discussed the major diseases like late blight, early blight, anthracnose, Fusarium
wilt, bacterial wilt, bacterial spot, Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus, pepper mosaic virus,
and nematode infestations, including their key symptoms and favorable conditions.
Abiotic disorders such as blossom-end rot, sunscald, and nutrient deficiencies are also
explained to avoid misdiagnosis.

To reduce losses, apply Integrated Disease Management (IDM), including the use of
disease-free seedlings, crop rotation, sanitation, resistant varieties, biological control
(Trichoderma, Bacillus), proper spacing, net houses, sticky traps, and appropriate
chemical control when needed.

Ender

Title: Stopping the Thieves
Time Allotment: 5 minutes
Materials Needed: Metacards, 5 permanent markers, board
Procedure:

1. Distribute metacards. Give each participant one metacard and a pen or
marker.
2. Explain the three categories
- START – New practices or habits they plan to begin doing after the
training.
- STOP – Practices or behaviors they realize are harmful or ineffective
and will stop doing.
- CONTINUE – Good practices or habits they are already doing and
should maintain or strengthen.

3. Ask the reflection question
Say: “After today’s training, what will you do differently in your own farm
or work to prevent these ‘unseen thieves’ from causing losses? It could
be something that you will START, STOP, or CONTINUE.”
4. Allow time to think and write. Give participants 3–5 minutes to write
their responses on the metacard. Encourage concise, actionable
statements
5. Posting responses. Ask participants to post their metacard under the
appropriate column (STOP, START, or CONTINUE) on the board.

Processing / Discussion
Once everyone has posted, read a few samples from each column. Highlight
patterns or common themes. Ask probing questions like:
- “Why did you choose to stop this practice?”
- “What support do you need to start doing this?”
- “What benefits have you seen from continuing this practice?”

Wrap-up / Synthesis
- Summarize the main takeaways:
- Reinforce good practices (Continue)
- Encourage commitment to new actions (Start)
- Emphasize the importance of letting go of harmful habits (Stop)

Statement to end the Lesson:
Change starts with awareness and grows through action. Let’s bring today’s
lessons to life by putting into practice what we’ll start, stop, and continue doing.
That’s how we’ll stop the ‘unseen thieves’ from stealing our hard work.

ANSWER KEY:

1. Late blight, Fusarium wilt, Bacterial wilt, Tomato leaf roll virus, Pepper
mosaic virus
2. Ralstonia solanacearum
3. - Cultural management (disease-free seeds or certified seedlings; Use of
grafted seedlings for soil-borne diseases; Crop rotation (avoid planting
solanaceous crops successively); Field sanitation (removal of infected
debris)
- Use of resistant varieties
- Use of biological control
- Use of chemical spray if necessary
4. - Observe symptoms. Look for yellowing, drooping, or sudden wilting of
leaves and stems.
- Uproot the affected plant carefully. Check the roots — if they are
dark, soft, or rotten, root rot may be the cause.
- Examine the stem. If roots are healthy, cut the stem and look for
brown discoloration in the vascular tissue.
- Water test for bacterial wilt. Cut a small section of the stem. Place it
in a clear glass of clean water. Wait for a few minutes. Bacterial ooze
coming out from the cut surface indicates bacterial wilt. No ooze
means it is likely Fusarium wilt.
- Confirm in the laboratory. Collect samples and send them to a plant
disease diagnostic laboratory for confirmation before recommending
any treatment

5. - I will regularly inspect my pepper and tomato plants for early signs of
disease.
- Avoid planting in the same area every season to reduce disease build-
up.
- Use disease-free seedlings and sterilized soil or seed trays.
- Improve field sanitation — remove and bury infected plants right
away.
- Practice proper watering to prevent excess moisture that favors
diseases.
- Apply Trichoderma or other beneficial microbes in the soil to
suppress pathogens.
- Ensure good spacing and airflow to keep the plants dry and healthy.
- Clean tools and equipment after use to avoid spreading diseases.

Lesson 8

Management of Pests of Tomato and Sweet Pepper

This lesson introduces the common pests affecting sweet pepper and tomato in the locality.
Recommended management practices to prevent early infestation and reduce population
of certain pests following Integrated Pest Management will be discussed. Synthetic
pesticides are commonly used by growers to control pests however, the importance of
integrating other practices to manage pest population and reduce their damage on the
plants will be presented. For successful management of pests, crop monitoring and
identification of pests is important.

At the end of the lesson, the participants should be able identity practices in
managing common pests attacking sweet pepper and tomato in their locality
and understand the importance of Integrating Pest Management.

2. discuss the different practices that could be used to manage pests on sweet
pepper and tomato.
3. decide what and when to apply management practices appropriate for certain

Lesson Proper

A. What is a Pest and Why Manage Pest?

Pest is any living organism that damages the plants and affects their growth and
development. Different pests could damage the plants by directly feeding or
destroying the parts of the plant and/or by transmitting plant diseases like virus
diseases which could also seriously affect the growth of the plants. Pests affecting
plants includes mites and different destructive insects (insect pests).

Pests affect the growth and development of plants and severe damage may cause poor
yield and low quality of produce resulting to low production and low or no income.
Not all pests could be totally controlled even with the use of pesticides however,
population and damage on the plants could be lowered using different inputs and
practices.

To start with, we will first discuss the type of pests and learn how to identify and
manage pests using different inputs and practices for the Integrated Management of
common pest attacking tomato and pepper.

1. Types of Pests
Pests affecting the plants could be classified as chewing, sucking or boring pests
based on their feeding characteristics.
a. Chewing pests – these pests damage the plants by consuming or chewing
the tissues of the plants mostly the leaves, flowers, fruits and young stem.
They have strong mouthparts which they use to cut and grind their food.
These are mostly insect pests like larvae or caterpillar, grubs and adult
beetles.
b. Sucking pests – these pests damage the plants by piercing plant tissues and
suck plant sap using their stylet or proboscis. Some of the sucking insect
pests also transmit diseases and inject toxins which affects the parts/plants
attacked.
c. Boring pests – these are chewing insects which tunnel into leaves, fruits and
stems of plants. These are mostly larval stages of some moth and butterflies;
and grubs and adult beetles feeding within the parts of the plants. The
common boring insect pests are leafminers, stem borers and fruit borers .

2. Pest identification
Common pests affecting plants could be identified through the following:
a. Plants attacked - Pests could be identified through the kind of plants
affected. Different plants usually have different pest problems.
b. Life stages and morphological characteristics of the pests - Pests may
develop through complete and incomplete metamorphosis and may
undergo 3-4 life stages with different characteristics which could be used in
identifying.
- Complete metamorphosis – pests undergo four life stages: egg, larva,
pupa and adult. These different stages have distinct morphological
characteristics and may feed on different parts of the plants. Example:
moth, butterflies, beetles
- Incomplete metamorphosis – pests undergo three stages: the egg,
nymph and adult. The nymph, which gradually increase in size after
hatching, are usually similar with the adult except for some

### PDF Page 162

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=162

undeveloped parts like wings and they also feed on the same part of the
plants. Example: aphids and mites
c. Pest damage observe on the plants or plant parts - Pests could be identified
through the damage observed on the different parts of the plants. The
chewing, sucking or boring pests causes different damage or symptoms on
the different parts of the plants they attack.

3. Management of pests
To manage pests, the following steps should be done:
a. Monitor farm and the plants (check stages of the plants, the practices
employed).
b. Monitor existing weather condition (temperature, rainfall, relative
humidity).
c. Check status or possible problems (area, plants, etc). Check possible damage
or symptoms on the plants.
d. If pest/s were monitored, identify the pests/s. Samples may be collected for
further identification or verification
e. Implement available and appropriate measures for specific problem/s
monitored.
f. Monitor implemented measures and status of the plants

Figure 62. Checking symptoms or damage on plants and Collecting plant samples for
further identification.

For better management of pests, Integrated Management must be implemented
following the recommended crop establishment and cultural management
practices to prevent early pest infestation and integrate other practices and
inputs to reduce the population and damage of certain pests.

These different practices and inputs could be as follows:
g. Follow crop establishment and cultural management practices
- Use of clean planting materials. To avoid early pest infestation after
transplanting, use clean and healthy planting materials. Check pest
incidence seedlings before transplanting.
- Use resistant varieties, if available.
- Select varieties to be planted. Consider the area to be planted, existing
climatic condition and production system to be followed.

### PDF Page 163

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=163

- Properly prepare the area and provide drainage.
- Properly establish the crop. Follow recommended planting distance,
time of planting and other establishment practices to prevent pest
problems.
- Maintain the crops following the recommended cultural management
practices like regular watering and weeding, proper fertilizer
application and regular training/pruning.

Figure 63. Healthy seedling for transplanting

h. Practice Crop Rotation
i. Removal and proper disposal of infested plants or plant parts. Prune or cut
few severely infested parts or plants to avoid further development and
spread of the pest.
j. Use of yellow sticky traps. These could be used under greenhouses or open
field to control population of adult stages of some pests like whiteflies and
leafminers.

Figure 64. Sample of yellow traps being used against whiteflies and leafminer

e. Use overhead or sprinkler irrigation. Population of some pests like
whiteflies, thrips and mites are reduce or wash out during overhead
irrigation.
f. Use biological control agents. Entomopathogenic fungi like Metarrhizium
anisopliae and Beauveria bassiana which are locally being produced could
be sprayed on the plants to manage population of soft bodied pests.

### PDF Page 164

Figure 65. Two (2) locally available entomopathogenic fungi for
biological control of some pest

g. Use of bio-pesticides. Available bio-pesticides could be used for some pests.
h. Regulated use of pesticides. Synthetic pesticides should be used as the last
resort. These toxic chemicals should be applied strictly following the
recommended rate and interval of application and avoid “cocktail”
application.

4. Common pests of tomato and pepper
The following are the common pests attacking tomato and pepper and their
management practices which include the use of clean planting materials and
proper establishment and management practices:

a. Aphids
Aphids are also called as plant lice and commonly called ”aplat”. Different
species attack pepper and tomato and they are usually colored green,
yellowish, grayish or black. They are mostly found on the shoots and other
young and succulent parts of the plants (leaves, flowers, fruits). Early
infestation and development usually starts on the underside of the leaves.
They pest multiply and infest the shoots and young leaves.

Figure 66. High population of aphids on the underside of the leaf (a) and shoots (b) of bell
pepper.

### PDF Page 165

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=165

Damage
- Aphids suck plant juice on young and tender parts of the plant resulting to
curling of shoots and high population at early stage may cause stunting.
- They produce sugary substance called honey dew and at high pest
population, black molds or sooty molds developed on severely infested
leaves/parts.
- Some species may transmit virus diseases on tomato like the Cucumber
Mosaic Virus -CMV

Figure 67. Sooty molds on leaves and fruits of sweet pepper due to high infestation of
pests aphids and also whiteflies.

Management practices
- Use healthy seedlings for transplanting.
- Regular weeding to remove alternate host plants
- Use yellow sticky trap to control adults.
- Removal and proper disposal of affected leaves, stems and fruits.
- Roguing and proper disposal of few severely attacked plants
- Use available bio-pesticide.
- Need-based use of synthetic insecticide.

b. Thrips
- These are tiny, soft-bodied sucking insect pests usually colored cream or
yellowish and hardly visible to the naked eye.
- Infestation is mostly observed on sweet pepper than tomato under local
condition.

Damage
- Mostly attack the shoots and young leaves and developing flowers and fruits.
They pierce and suck plant juice on surfaces of young leaves, flowers and
fruits.
- High population results to leaf curling and abnormal shape and silvery color
or bronzing of affected parts.
- Severe infestation during vegetative growth of plants results to stunting.
- Severe infestation during the early fruit development may cause fruit drop
due to drying and developing fruits are usually small and malformed with
brown or rusty skin color.

### PDF Page 166

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=166

Figure 68. Damage of thrips on sweet pepper from flowering to fruit development

Management practices
- Use healthy planting materials.
- Regular weeding to remove alternate host plants. Alternate hosts like potato,
onions and cucurbits should not be planted or rotated with sweet pepper and
tomato.
- Roguing of few severely attacked plants
- Overhead irrigation reduce population of thrips.
- Adjust planting dates to avoid peak of population.
- Spray biological control agents (Metarrhizium or Beauveria) and other bio-
pesticide.
- Spray recommended insecticide.

c. Mites
- These are tiny and soft bodied pests usually not visible to the naked eyes.
- Two spotted mites and red mites mostly attack sweet pepper and tomato under
local condition. They have different host plants and year round infestation may
occur especially under greenhouses with warm and dry condition.

Damage
- Infestation mostly starts on the lower leaves and later attacks the shoots and
young leaves. They suck plant juice from leaves and developing flowers and fruits
resulting to abnormal growth (deformed, leaf curling). Severe infestation results
to yellowing of leaves, drying of leaves and abnormal shaped fruits.

Figure 69. Different stages of two spotted mites On the underside of leaves (enlarged)

Figure 70. Tomato leaves severely infested with mites

Management practices
- Use healthy seedlings for transplanting
- Overhead irrigation and surface irrigation reduce pest population
- Regular irrigation stimulates growth of plants and damage during the stage when
plants are susceptible could be reduced/escaped
- Adjust planting dates to avoid peak of infestation which is mostly during dry and
hot condition
- Crop rotation
- Spray biological control agents (Metarrhizium anisopliae or Beauveria bassiana)
and other bio-pesticides.
- Spray acaricide/miticide.

d. Whiteflies
- These are tiny sucking insect pests. The wings and body are usually covered with
white waxy coatings and they adult and immature stages are usually found
developing and feeding on the underside of the leaves
- They attack different crops and population rapidly increases during warm and
dry condition. Infestation could be year round under greenhouses especially
with the continous cultivation of different host plants.

Figure 71. High population of adult and immature stages of whiteflies on the underside of
the leaves of pepper

Damage
- The pest sucks plant juice from the surfaces of leaves and also fruits and high
population may cause wilting and drying of plants.
- Severe infestation at early vegetative growth results to stunting and affected
fruits have abnormal shape.
- Growth of sooty (black) molds occur during high population causes stunting of
plants and poor quality fruits.
- Transmit important virus diseases of tomato and sweet pepper.

Management practices
- Use clean seedlings for transplanting
- Use yellow sticky traps
- Pruning or eradication of severely affected plants/parts
- Crop rotation. Avoid continous planting of other host pants especially under
greenhouses.
- Spray insecticide at early infestation where population is low.

e. Leafminer
- The small larvae mine and feed between the upper and lower surfaces of the
leaves, creating winding and whitish tunnels which are initially narrow which
later widen as the larvae feed and grow.

Damage
- Infested leaves dry and may drop prematurely and severely infested plants may
lose most of their leaves
- Heavy infestation during the early vegetative stage of plants results to stunting,
drying or death of plants

Summary

Different pests commonly attack sweet pepper and tomato from vegetative to fruiting
stage however, the population and degree of damage on the plants depends on different
factors like location, existing weather condition, varieties planted and the crop
management and pest management practices employed by growers.

For effective management of pests, pest monitoring and identification should be done; and
different practices and inputs should be used following Integrated Pest Management. This
is to reduce pest population and damage; and reduce or regulate the use of synthetic
pesticides which have different side effects to human and the environment.

Ender

Title: Match and Manage
Time Allotment: 5-10 minutes
Materials Needed: printed pest photos in half of A4 paper size; Management
Cards printed in half size of A4 paper size

Procedure:
1. Say: “Before we end our session, let’s review what we’ve learned about
identifying and managing pests in tomato and sweet pepper. This activity
will test how well you can connect what you see in the field with the right
management practice.”
2. Divide participants into small groups (3–5 members).
3. Give each group one set of pest photo cards and one set of management
cards.
4. Matching Activity
Say:“Each group should look at the pest or damage photo and choose the
best management card that fits. You can discuss with your group —
remember, some pests can have more than one management option, so
choose the most effective or practical one for your farm.”
5. Discussion and Review (3 minutes)
Ask groups to share one or two matches they made.
Facilitate a quick review:
o “Why did you choose that management method?”
o “What are other possible ways to manage this pest?”
o Provide short clarifications or corrections as needed
6. Conclude by saying:
“Great work, everyone! You’ve shown that proper pest identification and
choosing the right management method are key to protecting your
tomato and sweet pepper crops. Remember: observe early, act wisely,
and always aim for balanced pest control using integrated methods.”

Statement to end the Lesson:
“Today’s activity showed that effective pest management begins with good
observation. When we can identify the pest correctly, we can choose the best and
safest control method. Integrated pest management doesn’t rely only on spraying
— it combines prevention, monitoring, and proper action. This approach keeps
our crops healthy, protects the environment, and reduces production costs.”

Lesson 9

Planning of Cropping System

This lesson introduces key principle in planning cropping systems to maximize the use of
greenhouses, with a focus on achieving long-term harvests of tomato and sweet pepper.

Lesson Objective
At the end of the lesson, the participants should be able to plan the optimal
cropping system for their environment and for sustainable income that is less
susceptible to price fluctuations of produce.

Specifically, the participants should be able to:
1. discuss the fluctuations of market price of vegetables;
2. explain the growth period of each vegetable and their favorable environmental
conditions; and
3. Design an optimal cropping system

Time Allotment: 2 hours
Methodologies: Lecture-discussion, workshop
Tools to Use: Laptop, LCD projector, PowerPoint (PPT) presentation, Manila Paper

B. Fluctuation of Market Price
C. Growth Period of Vegetables
D. Examples of Cropping Systems
E. Examples of Net Profit/Cost Ratio

Title: Plan or Panic

Procedure
6. Say, ““Imagine you are going on a long trip tomorrow morning. You didn’t
check your vehicle, didn’t pack your things, and didn’t look up directions.
What might happen?”
7. Let a few participants respond
Common Answers: “You’ll get lost.” “You’ll forget something.” “You’ll waste

for their crops to avoid losses — this is called planning a cropping system.”

Key concepts to be derived:
- Good Planning Saves Time, Labor, and Money
- Preparing early — checking soil, choosing crops, and scheduling activities —

- Without planning, farmers often waste resources (seeds, fertilizer, fuel) and
time fixing problems that could have been avoided

Connecting statement to the Lesson:
“Today, we’ll learn how farmers plan their cropping systems — deciding what crops to
grow, when to plant them, and how to manage them to achieve good yield and income
despite unpredictable market conditions.”

Lesson Proper

A. Introduction
The market prices of vegetables often fluctuate with a great extent, and since most
vegetables have short shelf life, storing them for long periods is difficult. Because
price fluctuation patterns vary each year, it is often challenging to predict price
changes and determine the best harvest time.

For this reason, it can be risky to plan harvests targeting a specific market period. To
reduce the impact of sudden price drops, it is recommended to grow long-term
harvesting crops such as tomato or sweet pepper. A commodity with short growth
period, such as lettuce, can be grown in between those vegetables.

Furthermore, incorporating green manure crops into the cropping system helps
maintain good soil condition in greenhouse production. For more details about this
practice, refer to Lesson 1: Soil Conditioning Through Green Manure Crops.

B. Fluctuation of Market Price
The prices of fresh vegetables change drastically throughout the year, and the pattern
of price fluctuation varies from year to year, as shown in Figure 1 below. The figure
presents examples of farmgate prices of tomato and sweet pepper in Benguet
Province from 2020-2024. Typically, the price of sweet pepper tends to increase
toward the end of the year, especially during Christmas season as observed in 2020,
2022 and 2024. However, this trend is not consistent in 2021 and 2023, showing that
market behavior is unpredictable and can change depending on various factors such
as supply, demand and weather conditions.

More evidently, the price fluctuation patterns of both tomato and sweet pepper were

Those year-to-year variations are influenced by many factors, including weather

Data on monthly wholesale, retail, and farmgate prices of almost all agricultural

Because of these unpredictable price fluctuations, it is advisable to plan for a longer
harvesting period, such as six (6) months, to help minimize the negative impact of
sudden price drops. For example, if tomatoes are harvested from July to December,
the crop has a greater chance of coinciding with a price peak at some point during the
season.

C. Growth Period of Vegetables
To plan the cropping system for greenhouse cultivation, it is necessary to understand
the growth period and characteristics of each vegetable particularly Tomato and
Sweet Pepper.

Tomato
Tomato plants are neutral plants which do not respond to photoperiod (day
length). They can grow in throughout the year as long as temperature conditions
are favorable. This makes tomato cultivation well-suited for greenhouse
cultivation in highland areas, such as Benguet Province.

On average, it takes about 60 days from sowing to the first flower bloom, and
another 60 days from flowering to harvest maturity. Thus, the total period from
sowing to the first harvest is approximately four (4) months. Generally, higher
temperatures shorten the period to harvest.

Under the common practices in the Philippines, the seedling-raising period is
about 45 days, whether using grafted or non-grafted seedlings. In grafted tomato
production, grafting is usually done 30 days after sowing, followed by 15 days of
post-grafting care. See Lesson 3: Grafting of Tomato Seedlings for more details.

When indeterminate tomato varieties are used, the harvest period can extend up
to six (6) months, as observed in the MV2C project. Achieving this requires
proper management of pests and diseases to maintain plant vigor throughout the
production cycle. Refer to Lesson 7 and Lesson 8 for guidance on pest and disease
control.

Sweet pepper
Sweet pepper plants are also neutral plants which do not respond to
photoperiod. They are well-suited for long-term harvest cultivation under
greenhouse conditions in highland areas.

Compared to tomatoes, sweet pepper generally takes longer to produce for their
first flowers. In the Philippines, bell type sweet peppers generally requires more
time from flowering to harvest, especially when waiting for fruit ripening and
color development (red, yellow, or orange). In contrast, Japanese-type sweet
peppers, which are smaller and have thinner skins, mature more quickly.

Approximately, sowing seeds to the first flower blooming takes 70 days, and
another 80days from flowering to harvest. If full color development is desired,
the period from flowering extends to 90 days. Therefore, it takes about 5 months
from sowing to the first harvest. The higher the temperature, the shorter the
period to harvest.

In common Philippine practice, the seedling-raising period for sweet pepper is
45 days.

Lettuce
In the MV2C pilot projects, both Romaine lettuce and broccoli were tried before
or after tomato and sweet pepper production. Results showed broccoli required
a long growing period – about 110 days (with a tested variety) from sowing to
harvest.

### PDF Page 182

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=182

In contrast, Romaine lettuce proved better suited to this cropping system,
especially when soil conditioning with green manure crops was practiced.
Romaine lettuce also offers a shorter growing period than head lettuce, typically
50-70 days from sowing to harvest.

Under common practices in the Philippines, the period of raising seedling is
about 20-25 days.

Green manure crops
The MV2C project promotes the use of soil conditioning using green manure
crops as same soil needs to be sustainably used for vegetable cultivation under
greenhouses.

The duration of green manuring depends on the crop type, but generally takes
about 2.5 - 3 months from sowing to soil incorporation. After the green manure
is incorporated, decompose before planting vegetable seedlings. For detailed
information on this practice, refer to Lesson1: Soil Conditioning Through Green
Manure Crops.

D. Examples of Cropping Systems
Figure 3 below shows examples of suggested cropping systems with long-term
harvest of tomato or sweet pepper. Cropping system “A” is a practice of crop rotation
with green manure crop, Romaine lettuce and tomato or sweet pepper. With this
system, tomato or sweet pepper can be harvested from late July to December.
Cropping system “B” includes intercropping of Romaine lettuce and tomato or sweet
pepper. With this, tomato or sweet pepper can be harvested from late June to
December, and if the plants are still manageable, harvest can still be continued until
January.

Sweet pepper plants are planted with a wide space between plants, making them
suitable for intercropping with lettuce. Refer to Lesson 5: Sweet Pepper Cultivation
Method for Long-term Harvesting for the detailed information on this practice. This
method is used to maximize the space in greenhouses.

E. Examples of Net Profit/Cost Ratio
Table 1 below shows successful performance of tomato and sweet pepper farming
tried in the pilot projects of MV2C. The following are the results of the pilot projects:

### PDF Page 183

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=183

- The longest harvest periods of tomato and sweet pepper were 6 months and 10
months, respectively.
- Yields of both vegetables were higher than the national average. The national
average yield of tomato is 14.7 t/ha and that of pepper (chili and bell pepper) is
4.6 t/ha (2023, FAOSTAT).
- Prices greatly fluctuated. The highest price was 10 times higher than the lowest
price in some cases.
- By applying the long-term harvest techniques, the farmers were not severely
affected by the extreme price fluctuation.
- Several farms recorded very high net-profit/cost ratio.
- The net-profit/cost ratio was influenced not only by yield and price but also by
production costs (not shown in the table).
- The main issues were damages caused by (1) typhoon and (2) diseases. Some
farmers had to give up the cultivation.

### PDF Page 184

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=184

Summary

The lesson discussed the importance of efficient cropping systems to maximize the use of
space and time within a greenhouse. It also explained advantages of long-term harvest
cultivation of tomato and sweet pepper with data of price fluctuation. It suggested the need
to understand the characteristics of target vegetables, such as growing period and
required planting density, to design an optimal cropping system.

Greenhouses are a precious facility/tool for farmers, and making the best use of them can
be key to successful farming. It needs to be noted that these practices are possible in rather
cool areas. This technology is not suitable for areas where the temperature inside the
greenhouse becomes too high. Further attempts will be needed to adapt it to low lands of
the country.

### PDF Page 185

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=185

Ender

Title: From Plan to Practice
Time Allotment: 5-7 minutes
Materials Needed: Metacards

Procedure:
1. Recall the Opening Activity: “At the start of our session, we imagined
what would happen if we went on a trip without a plan — we said we’d
get lost, waste time, or spend more. Farming works the same way.”
2. Connect to the Lesson: “Today, we learned that planning a cropping
system means preparing what to plant, when to plant, and how to
maintain soil health and income throughout the year. Just like planning
a journey, we make fewer mistakes when we plan our crops carefully.”
3. Reflection Question. Ask the participants:
- “What part of your farm do you think you can plan better next
season?”
- “How can planning help you avoid panic when prices drop or
weather changes?”
Let 2–3 participants share short answers.
4. Ask participants to finish this sentence using their METACARDS:
“To avoid panic in farming, I will plan for ________.”
(Examples: “soil preparation,” “seed selection,” “harvest timing,” “market
schedule.”)

Processing and Statement to end the Lesson:

“When we plan, we don’t panic — we act with purpose.
A well-planned cropping system helps us use our land wisely, earn more steadily,
and protect our soil for the next season. Farming success starts not in the field, but
in good planning.”

### PDF Page 186

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-003 | document=DA & JICA MV2C Training Module on Long-Term Harvesting of Tomato and Sweet Pepper | pdf_page=186

SELF-ASSESSMENT

1. Why is it important for farmers to plan their cropping system?
a) To make planting more expensive
b) To increase risks and uncertainty
c) To use land, time, and resources more efficiently
d) To plant only one crop all year round
2. What is one main reason why crop planning should consider market price
trends?
a) Prices are always the same each year
b) Market prices of vegetables can fluctuate unpredictably
c) Farmers cannot sell their crops in the market
d) Prices are not important to farmers
3. What is the advantage of combining short-term crops like lettuce with long-
term crops like tomato or sweet pepper?
a) It reduces soil fertility
b) It allows continuous harvest and income
c) It delays land use
d) It increases pest attacks
4. How does soil pH relate to crop planning?
a) It tells farmers when to irrigate
b) It affects nutrient availability for crops
c) It measures temperature of the soil
d) It controls insect population
5. What can happen if a farmer plants without proper planning?
a) Higher yields and profits
b) Efficient resource use
c) Wasted time, money, and poor harvest
d) Better market timing

ANSWERS with EXPLANATIONS:

1. C - Planning helps farmers make efficient use of land, labor, and inputs while
minimizing risks.
2. B - Prices of vegetables change every year and season, so planning helps
farmers avoid selling during price drops.
3. B - Planting crops with different growth periods ensures continuous production
and better income stability.
4. B - Soil pH affects the availability of nutrients — even if nutrients are present,
plants can’t absorb them if pH is too high or too low.
5. C - Lack of planning can lead to poor timing, soil problems, or low market prices
— resulting in losses.

for all involved.

Rice is the most important cereal staple crop in the Philippines. It is attacked
by many harmful organisms throughout the country at its different stages of
growth, but only a few of these organisms are of national and location-specific
importance. This field guide provides diagnostic information, short descriptions
of the most important species, their identification marks, the ecosystem they
dominate, the nature of damage inflicted, their biology, and the management
options to employ.

These information will help extension workers, farmers, and nonspecialists
identify the harmful and useful organisms in rice fields. Colored photographs
are provided for easy identification of the organisms. Appropriate control
measures are suggested. It is clear that most pest outbreaks are induced by
poor management practices. Close monitoring and early recognition of poten
tial pest species will be useful in future pest management programs.

INTRODUCTION

This field guide is designed to assist agricultural technologists, farmers,
students, and nonspecialists identify the most common harmful and
helpful organisms found in Philippine rice fields.

Not all organisms are pests; many are useful because they feed on pest
species. Some of the more easily visible useful organisms are described
in this guide to emphasize that it is important to determine the roles of
organisms found on crops, rather than to assume that all organisms are
harmful and so must be eliminated! In fact there are more species that are
helpful than harmful ones.

As this guide is aimed for use by nontaxonomists, we have strived to use
nontechnical terms, as it is not always easy to identify living organisms from
photographs.

For the harmful organisms, the most characteristic identification marks,
the ecosystem they dominate, the damage they inflict, and their life cycles
are illustrated and described together with suggestions or management
options, where appropriate.

This reference will be a useful tool to contribute further to the application
of Integrated Crop Management (ICM) technologies to raise production
levels, maximize profits, and reduce populations of harmful organisms
through nonchemical methods. Chemical control should be used only
where essential, and preferably with the advice of a local crop protection
specialist.

The users of this field guide are advised to have the diseased
specimens/tissues further examined under the microscope and by
laboratory tests conducted by crop protection specialists to confirm
the field diagnoses.

### PDF Page 6

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-005 | document=Field Guide: Harmful and Useful Organisms in Philippine Rice Fields - Insects and Non-Insects | pdf_page=6

HOW TO USE THIS FIELD GUIDE

Decision-making is the backbone of ICM. Correct and timely decision in
ICM is only possible when the nonspecialist has a thorough knowledge of
both living and nonliving organisms in the rice ecosystem. An individual
entering a rice field usually encounters living organisms, which are either
harmful (those feeding on parts of the rice plant) or useful (those feeding
on harmful organisms). One should take note of the following: the plant
growth stage, the plant part where it is found, and its activity (feeding on
the plant or feeding on other organisms). Integrated Pest Management
(IPM) is an integral component of ICM, which looks at the ecosystem in
totality. The major emphasis is on weekly monitoring of the rice fields,
taking into account the abundance of useful organisms along with the
numbers of harmful organisms, plant growth stage, water status, leaf color,
and general crop growth status.

Harmful organisms can be broadly grouped further into two categories:
insects (six-legged) and non-insects, which comprise those without a
backbone (e.g., earthworms, snails) and those with a backbone (e.g., rats,
birds). The harmful insects are further grouped based on two criteria: plant
part they feed on (root, leaf, stem, sap, grain) and the degree of economic
importance (color-coded as follows: red for most harmful, orange
for harmful but location-specific, and yellow for less harmful). Useful
organisms have either six legs (insects), eight legs (web and non-web-
forming spiders), or no legs (white/green fungus, viruses). They can be
grouped further based on the following criteria: habitat occupied (color-
coded as follows: green for aerial-borne organisms, blue for water-
borne organisms, and white for insect-killing fungus, bacterium, and
virus) and visible mobility (mobile are insects and spiders; mobility not
visible in insect-killing fungus, bacterium, and virus).

On establishing the identity of the harmful organisms, refer for more
detailed information on the local name, identification marks, rice ecosystem
it dominates, nature of damage inflicted, life cycle, and management
strategies. Similarly, for useful organisms refer for details on the local name,
identification marks, rice ecosystem, food as prey, and life cycle.

The last section of the field guide provides information on:
- cultural practices useful in the management of harmful insects;
- scientific and local names of the organisms;
- pest abundance and rice susceptibility;
- popular Philippine rice varieties and their agronomic characteristics and
pest and disease reactions; and
- glossary of terms used in this field guide.

HARMFUL ORGANISMS
CATEGORY: INSECTS (SIX-LEGGED ORGANISMS)

ROOT FEEDERS

Mole Cricket
Tagalog name: susuhong

Mole cricket damage (inset) to rice
at early vegetative stage

The insect is light brown; its wings are folded and do not cover the full
length of the abdomen. The forelegs are broad, curved, with strong teeth-
like structures for digging soil. The hind legs, eyes, and antennae are small
and almost invisible. The adult is 25-35 millimeters (mm) long.

They live in all rice environments but are most prevalent in non-flooded
upland rice fields with damp soil. They are usually found in burrows along
the levees or shelter in seedbeds during daytime. Heaps of soil mark the
entrances to extensive burrows in the soil. They prefer moist soils with high
organic matter. In areas where the dry season is short, they can multiply
in unusually large numbers. They cannot survive in the rice fields after
flooding.

Damage:
Mole cricket damage is greater near the field borders where they relocate
after tillage operations. Susceptible growth stages are from seedling to
tillering. At night, adults and nymphs feed on sown seeds and roots of rice
plants either in the seedbed or of young seedlings, causing bare patches
in the field. In older plants, tillers near the soil surface may be chewed
on, but the damage can generally be tolerated. Young and newly planted
seedlings are most commonly attacked in the early part of the season
before fields are flooded.

### PDF Page 10

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-005 | document=Field Guide: Harmful and Useful Organisms in Philippine Rice Fields - Insects and Non-Insects | pdf_page=10

Life cycle:
Females burrow bunds
and construct hardened
cells in which eggs are laid.
Each cell contains 30-50 adult
eggs. Depending on the egg
temperature, eggs hatch in
15-40 days. Their capacity
to migrate is limited. They
also eat each other. Nymphs 3-4 mos nymph 15-40 days
become adults in 3-4 months.
Adults are attracted to light
traps.

Management options: Life cycle of a mole cricket

Cultural
- Bund-shaving and plastering with fresh wet soil kills their eggs.
- Levelling fields provides better water control, which can limit mole
cricket invasions.
- Collecting nymphs and adults during land preparation, bund repairs,
and seedling pulling in nursery beds reduce their population.
- Maintaining standing water in the field prevents their damage.
- After rains, they are attracted to light sources during nighttime. They
can then be collected, destroyed, and even eaten.
- Varieties with long and dense fibrous root systems like many of the
modern varieties tolerate damage better.

Biological
- They eat each other when they are together. Hence, they regulate their
own numbers.
- Nymphs and adults have many natural enemies such as big wasps and
nematodes.

Chemical
- Poisoned baits made of mixed moistened rice bran and insecticide,
placed along rice bunds or drier areas of the field, kill night-foraging
mole crickets.
- Granular insecticides are effective but expensive; foliar insecticides are
ineffective.

LEAF FEEDERS

Leaf folder
Tagalog names: mambibilot, maniniklop

The adults are light brown moths with a
wingspan of 12-20mm. A dark terminal band
characterizes the outer margins of the wings.
Larvae are transparent green and measure up to
2.5 centimeters (cm) in length. Adults are
attracted to light at night; at daytime, they are
mostly found in shaded or grassy areas.

Leaffolders live in all environments but
are abundant during the rainy season.
High humidity, shady areas of the 6-8 (a)
field, and excessive use of nitrogenous days
fertilizers favor their rapid multiplication.

Damage: (b)
Leaffolders inflict damage in the larva
stage. Plants are susceptible to attack
up to 10 weeks after transplanting (i.e.,
from seedling to flowering). Infestation (c)
usually occurs during early growth adult
stages of the rice crop. The larvae infest
the leaves of young plants; they fasten
pupa eggthe edges of a leaf together and live
inside the rolled leaf. Heavy infestation
makes the plant look burnt, sickly, and
twig-like.
4-7

the young leaves. They are flat, oval,
15-25and whitish yellow. Eggs hatch to larvae
daysin 4-7 days. The transparent green, slender larvae
feed inside the folded leaves for 15-25 days before

Total life cycle takes 25-52 days. For adult moths, (a)(b) CnaphalocrocisMarasmia exigua,medinalis(c) Marasmia patnalis

### PDF Page 12

> RAG locator: source_id=AGRI-005 | document=Field Guide: Harmful and Useful Organisms in Philippine Rice Fields - Insects and Non-Insects | pdf_page=12

Management options:
Modern rice varieties and conservation of useful organisms, coupled with
location-specific cultural management practices, can regulate leaffolder
population without resorting to chemicals.

Cultural
- Clipping tops of bundled seedlings before transplanting removes eggs.
- Removing weeds prevents leaffolder buildup.
- Reducing amount of nitrogenous fertilizer and splitting the application
make rice plants less favorable for egg-laying and leaffolder attack.
- Potassium makes cell walls thicker because of greater silica uptake,
making the plant more tolerant to leaffolders.
- Higher infestation occurs in shady places.
- Wider spacing reduces infestation.
- Early planting enables plants to escape a high degree of defoliation.
- Most modern rice varieties can compensate for leaffolder defoliation;
making insecticides no longer necessary for control.
- Varieties with narrow leaves are more resistant to leaffolders than
varieties with wider leaves.

Biological
- Small wasps and crickets kill leaffolder eggs.
- Big wasps, damselflies, ants, and carabid (guitar) beetles prey on larvae.
- During the wet season, frequent moderate rainfall enables pathogens
to wipe out the entire larval population. Fungi and nuclear polyhydrosis
virus (NPV) kill the larvae.
- Spiders eat adult leaffolders.

Caseworm/Case Bearer
Tagalog names: uod na nasa supot

The adults are small, delicate, snowy-white moths with pale brown or black
spots on the wings. They have a wingspan of 15-25mm. Larvae are pale
translucent green, with a pale orange head. There are easy early detection
methods to know the pest activity in the area. Moths are attracted to light
traps, which also indicate whether there is pest activity in the area.

Caseworm is found in irrigated and wetland areas where standing water
in the field is a prerequisite for larval survival. The infestation is severe on
dwarf, compact, heavy-tillering, and high-yielding varieties during the rainy
season. Defoliation occurs before maximum tillering of rice.

Caseworm damage. Note the cut leaf cases and standing water.

Damage:
The larva is the damaging stage. The larvae cut the tip of the leaves,
as though by scissors, to make floating cases. They use these cases as
a reservoir of water, for breathing, and to protect themselves against
predators. The cases also facilitate their dispersal through flowing water
and wind. During the day, the larvae remain inside the case and float on the
water surface. At night, they feed on the lower side of leaves lying flat on
the water, or on submerged leaves. In general, a young vigorously growing
crop recovers from defoliation, but maturity may be delayed by 7-10 days.
In heavily infested crops, however, the loss of photosynthetic tissue can
be critical and seedlings may die. Older plants are generally more tolerant
to damage, and mature plants are seldom attacked. Susceptible growth
stages are from seedling to tillering.

Adults can live up to 3 weeks and are attracted to light traps.

Management options:

Cultural
- Transplanting older seedlings limits the period of larval attack.
- Draining the field for several days kills caseworm larvae.
- Sparse planting reduces damage.

Biological
- Big wasps and water beetles kill larvae.
- Spiders, dragonflies, and birds prey on the adults.

Chemical
- Caseworm larvae are highly susceptible to foliar and granular
insecticides. Apply insecticides only to fields with standing water and
only when larvae are present.

Skipper

Larva of skipper and its
damage on rice leaf

Adults of rice skipper

The adult is a stout brown butterfly with small white spots on the wings.
Adults are active during the day, making darting, erratic movements from
which the name skipper was coined. Adults rest in the shade during
the day. Larvae are elongated with a constriction behind the head
accentuating their flattened shape.

They occur in all rice environments, but prevalent in rainfed rice. Upland
environments with their diverse microhabitats can provide more favorable sites
than lowland rice plains. In some cases, upland rice is most affected. Droughts,
downpours, floods, or misuse of pesticides can cause their outbreaks because
useful organisms regulating them get depleted.

Damage:
Defoliation is the first sign of the presence of skipper larvae. The larvae are
difficult to see because they hide in the leaf tubes and feed mostly at night.
Damage occurs in patches or clusters, around where females lay their eggs.
Damage is not uniformly dispersed across a field. The larvae feed on leaves
from the margins inwards and then parallel to the midrib. In addition, the
larvae tie with silken threads the two edges of the same leaf or two adjacent
leaves to form a tube in which they live. Generally one larva is found in a fold.
Damage is severe in young transplanted rice seedlings and the attack may
continue until the plant matures. In severe cases, the plant does not recover.
This pest adversely affects grain quality.

- Dense cropping and good fertilization are important. Do not overuse
or underuse nitrogen fertilizer. The experience of progressive farmers in
the area can provide guidelines on the amount and number of fertilizer

Whorl Maggot
Tagalog names: langaw palay, langaw bukid

Adult flies are dull grey. Females are 1.8mm-2.3mm long. Males are slightly
shorter.

It is a pest of rice seedlings only under irrigated and rainfed conditions.
Adults prefer ponds, streams, lakes, and irrigated rice fields for their
breeding. This is because the adults locate rice fields by reflected sunlight
from the water surface. Hence, direct-seeded fields or seedbeds are not
seriously damaged. Rice crop with a mat of azolla on the water surface
repels egg-laying of adult flies. In addition, once the plant canopy closes,
they can no longer find the rice crop. Rice plants grown under continuous
standing water in the first 3-4 weeks after transplanting have more damage
than plants in fields where the soil is only saturated. When the young plants
are simultaneously stressed with either soil mineral deficiencies or toxicities
and other biotic stresses (caseworm or stem borer), the plants damaged by
whorl maggots cannot recover; and thus, yield loss will be high.

Damage:
The larva that causes damage is called the maggot. It feeds on unopened
leaves, nibbling the inner margins. When the leaves emerge from the
whorl, damage can be seen as pinhole feeding areas on the leaves, with
conspicuous white and yellowish linear patches near the edge of leaves.
Severely damaged leaves become distorted and may break from the wind.
Infested plants are stunted with few tillers. Susceptible growth stages are
seedling to tillering. However, the pest can cause damage to the boot leaf
and developing panicles, which can lead to only partial filling of the grains.
Crop maturation may be delayed up to 2 weeks; thereby, increasing the risk
of crop exposure to typhoons and other stresses.

Management options
Life cycle of a whorl maggot
Cultural
- Densely planted seedbeds do not attract adult flies.
- Transplanting older seedlings (25-30 days) avoids damage.
- Draining the field at 3-4 day intervals during the first 30 days after
transplanting reduces egg-laying.
- Adults are not attracted to light traps, and they feed on decaying
matter.
- Direct seeding discourages maggot buildup because the plant covers
the water surface more rapidly.
- Dense planting decreases egg-laying.
- Plants that cover the water surface such as azolla help prevent
infestation.
- More potassium increases plant tolerance to maggots, as cell walls get
thicker because of greater silica uptake.
- Adult flies are strongly attracted to fishmeal baits.
- High-tillering varieties are more tolerant than low-tillering varieties.

Biological
- Small wasps and field crickets kill eggs.
- Big wasps kill maggots.
- Water-borne and aerial-borne spiders eat adults.

Chemical
- Maggot control in seedbed is less expensive. Treat seedlings by soaking
them overnight in a slurry of systemic insecticide and zinc oxide (ZnO2)
powder solution before transplanting.
- Broadcast granules or mix systemic granules during the last harrowing
before transplanting.
- Foliar sprays are effective only at 1-2 weeks after transplanting (WAT).
